fullText:
MOSCOW, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Russia's health watchdog said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among people who had come ‌into contact with a Siberian plague institute laboratory worker who died ‌last week.

Authorities say the 28-year-old woman died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in ​a case that has prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump.

Rospotrebnadzor, the watchdog, said in a statement that no infectious diseases had been reported among the staff of the same plague research institute in Irkutsk over the past 10 ‌days and that extensive testing ⁠had found no microorganisms in the deceased woman's body linked to her work.

Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, ⁠where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said that what she called "a dangerous diagnosis" had not been confirmed.

She added that 60% of those placed under quarantine as ​a ​precaution had already been released. Local media ​said around 200 people had previously ‌been quarantined.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov expressed appreciation for an offer of help on Monday from Trump, although without making clear if Moscow planned to accept it.

"It's always good when mutual assistance is offered," Peskov told reporters.

He said the public health watchdog was handling the situation and would provide further information as it became available.

Trump ‌on Monday described the situation as a "big problem ​for Russia". US Secretary of State Marco ​Rubio said on Tuesday it was ​incumbent on Moscow to share more information.

World Health Organization spokesperson ‌Christian Lindmeier said on Tuesday that Russian ​authorities had yet to ​officially respond to a WHO request for information about the death of the lab worker.

"All of the patient's contacts have been reportedly identified and ​are being monitored for illness, ‌and none to date have shown symptoms of illness," he said.

(Reporting ​by Vladimir Soldatkin, Anastasia Lyrchikova and Andrew Osborn; Writing by Maxim ​Rodionov and Mark TrevelyanEditing by Andrew Osborn )

title: NI make huge strides despite Georgia frustration
description: With eight points from four games, Northern Ireland show real progress through what manager Michael O'Neill calls "one of the most enjoyable windows" he has had in international football.
fullText:
Northern Ireland's first nine points in the Uefa Nations League were accumulated over the grand total of 17 games.

Finishing their four-game window with a stalemate against Georgia on Monday night ensured Michael O'Neill's side earned eight across a mere 11 days.

It says plenty about the growing mood around this young side that, even after what was undoubtedly their best ever Nations League window, fans filed out of Windsor Park frustrated that it was not more.

Isaac Price's saved penalty in the 83rd minute was naturally the most glaring missed opportunity to take all three points in a second consecutive goalless draw in Belfast after Hungary also left with a point last week.

There had been other good chances, though, with Paddy Kelly and Josh Magennis both unable to capitalise on promising positions, while Ruairi McConville hit the bar in the incident that led to the penalty.

Magennis himself summed up the general mood at the final whistle when he told BBC Sport NI he was "bitterly disappointed" to take only a point from the game.

When the dust settles, however, the block as a whole can only be considered a success.

Two weeks ago, Northern Ireland were yet to win a game in the second tier of the Nations League and had never picked up all three points on their travels at any level of the competition.

Away victories in Georgia and against Ukraine in Slovakia both felt like huge steps forward for a side whose average age was as low as 22 in the latter fixture which they won 3-0.

On top of that, four successive clean sheets ensured they are the only team in the competition yet to concede a goal, all the more impressive considering that Conor Bradley remains on the sidelines and Daniel Ballard was only fit to feature in the first game.

"It was a hard camp, a lot different to what any of us have experienced before, and I thought we dealt with it really well," said Fulham midfielder Shea Charles who, along with Trai Hume, displayed Premier League pedigree throughout the window.

"We've won two away games, drew two at home, no goals conceded, there's not many complaints. I think we've been really good."

With this new four-game window presenting something different for managers across Europe to tackle, a myriad of approaches emerged.

Germany boss Jurgen Klopp named virtually two separate squads for his side's two pairs of games, while Ukraine made 10 changes between their first two games and then nine for their defeat by Northern Ireland.

Having spoken before the start of the campaign about how the condensed schedule would be more difficult for smaller nations, O'Neill kept changes to a minimum.

He started only 15 different players across the four games with two of his changes enforced by Ballard's injury and Ethan Galbraith's absence against Ukraine to attend the birth of his child.

Despite the relatively small pool of starters, this still feels like a window when Northern Ireland's depth was tested and passed with flying colours.

O'Neill was without talisman Bradley and the reliable Ali McCann coming into the window, and then lost Ballard to a hamstring injury after the first game in Tbilisi.

Young centre-backs McConville, 21, and Tom Atcheson, 20, looked ready to play at this level, while Ciaron Brown started all four games and drew plaudits having often had to bide his time in past squads.

Kieran Morrison, Terry Devlin and Brodie Spencer all impressed when given a chance against Ukraine.

O'Neill's praise for his squad is across the board.

"For me it's been one of the most enjoyable windows I've had as an international manager, and that's been because of the players," said O'Neill.

"How they've applied themselves, how desperate they are to do well, that's a real positive.

"We've a brilliant group of players and a lot of them I think will play international football for a long time."

Despite what will feel like two points dropped against Georgia, the team remains top of Group B2 before next month's concluding fixtures at home to Ukraine and away to Hungary.

Having already secured their League B status at the very least, back-to-back Nations League promotions and second seeding in December's Euro 2028 qualifying draw remain on the table.

In a broader sense, the past 11 days have served to heighten the growing excitement around the team's direction of travel.

"Honestly, the sky's the limit," said Magennis.

"I think they've probably got maybe four tournaments to have a crack at. The group's in a fantastic place."

If O'Neill was slightly more coy, he echoed the general sentiment.

"I know what the potential of this team is, I'm not always going to share that with you guys if I'm honest," concluded the manager.

"For me the team is maturing and growing and progressing all the time. It's good that the fans are excited, that's what we want. We want them to look at this team and be proud.

"I know these boys over the last two or three years, I've seen them grow. I see them with each other, which is really important and this team shows all the best sides of Northern Ireland."

fullText:
The Seattle Seahawks are in the process of adding running back Joe Mixon to their practice squad after working him out Monday, coach Mike Macdonald said, and early takes from people on social media weighed his health against Seattle's crowded backfield.

NFL insider Jordan Schultz reported on Monday that Seattle is signing Mixon, who will wear jersey No. 25. ESPN's Adam Schefter reported that the plan is to sign the veteran running back to the practice squad once he completes his medical exam.

Mixon, a two-time Pro Bowler, missed all of 2025 with a foot injury, and the Houston Texans released him in March. Texans general manager Nick Caserio called the injury "kind of a freak thing" in January.

In July, KPRC-2 Houston's Aaron Wilson reported that Mixon had told former Bengals teammates he was done playing and that he had dealt with blood flow problems in his foot and had recently undergone another surgery on it. He added that a source close to Mixon still saw some hope of a return.

SleeperSeahawks, a Seahawks news account, was struck by how quickly things changed over the last 48 hours. "He must be healthy!" SleeperSeahawks wrote.

Fox Sports' Jay Glazer had reported a day earlier that Seattle was bringing Mixon in for a visit. Schultz reported later Monday that Seattle wanted to make sure Mixon was in shape and came away impressed with his conditioning, and that Mixon will start on the practice squad.

A fan drew the same conclusion about the foot. "They wouldn't sign Mixon if the foot was bad," the fan wrote, adding that a healthy Mixon could earn a real role fast.

Mixon was productive the last time he played. He ran for 1,016 yards, 15th in the NFL, and 11 touchdowns on 245 carries for Houston in 2024, and he has 7,428 career rushing yards in 111 games. His last game was a Divisional Round playoff game at Kansas City on Jan. 18, 2025.

Seattle ON Tap, a Seattle sports fan account, expressed surprise and hope for a healthy Mixon in his prime. "Did not think this would actually happen," Seattle ON Tap wrote.

Seattle also has a need at the position. The defending Super Bowl champions, 3-1 after Sunday's 30-23 win over the Los Angeles Chargers, put first-round rookie Jadarian Price on injured reserve Saturday with a chest injury, and Kenneth Walker III, the Super Bowl MVP, signed with the Kansas City Chiefs in March.

One fan, replying to Schefter's report, wrote that a practice-squad start for a two-time Pro Bowler shows Seattle "wants to see the legs before handing him anything." The fan called it a low-risk move with Price on injured reserve.

Mixon would join the backfield Emanuel Wilson carried against the Chargers. Wilson, who is ranked 42nd on PFN's RB Impact Metric, ran 21 times for 81 yards and a touchdown and caught three passes for 39 yards and another score, while George Holani had 18 yards on seven carries.

FantasyPros analyst Derek Brown was blunter. "A mess of a backfield gets even messier," Brown wrote.

Charbonnet is working back, too. He tore his ACL in January's Divisional Round win over the San Francisco 49ers, had surgery on Feb. 20, and returned to practice Thursday.

"He's going to get team reps this week, which is really exciting," Macdonald told Seattle Sports' Brock and Salk on Monday. He also said Charbonnet will not play against the 49ers in Week 5.

"Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet fantasy managers watching the Seahawks sign Joe Mixon," Yahoo Fantasy Sports wrote.

Mixon is not headed straight to the active roster. Macdonald said he would join the practice squad, and Schefter reported that Mixon was still completing his medical exam on Monday.

title: Accept ‘bad things’ in return for benefits of AI, says Sam Altman
description:
Boss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliver
Sam Altman says he believes the world should accept “bad things” happening with AI in exchange for the benefits of the technology.
The chief executive of OpenAI cited hacks, scams and “other bad things that will happen” in an interview that sparked an instant backlash from critics of the big AI companies. His comments came after one of his company’s safety experts resigned, saying at the weekend that its “culture is broken”.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Boss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliver

Sam Altman says he believes the world should accept “bad things” happening with AI in exchange for the benefits of the technology.

The chief executive of OpenAI cited hacks, scams and “other bad things that will happen” in an interview that sparked an instant backlash from critics of the big AI companies. His comments came after one of his company’s safety experts resigned, saying at the weekend that its “culture is broken”.

In an interview released on Monday, Altman was asked about how OpenAI’s approach to safety differed from that of Anthropic, which has called for the industry to slow down after one of its researchers quit, warning that AI experts believed “it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

“I think there’s a lot of daylight,” Altman said. “One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use AI widely].

“I do think the lighter touch regulatory stance we advocate for comes with an accepting of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience.

“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying we will make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams or all the other bad things that will happen because I think that people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude – more good stuff than bad stuff.”

The interview for Politico’s Decoded podcast drew a strong response from Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida. He said he had “no dice” with the idea “a handful of tech oligarchs get to make that decision [on safety] for the rest of us”.

His state last week asked a judge to bar OpenAI from developing new AI models without third-party approved guardrails.

Gary Marcus, a prominent AI sceptic and professor emeritus at New York University, said Altman was “saying the quiet part out loud: suck it up, so you can make us rich and powerful”.

Altman also reignited a feud with Elon Musk, telling Vanity Fair: “I don’t like bullies, and I think Elon’s a bully.”

He had been asked if the AI industry could “grow up” and work together.

“I think once in a while you got to punch a bully back in the nose,” Altman said. “And I also think Elon, like many bullies, only respects people who do. So if you want me to be able to work with him, maybe you should be happy I hit back once in a while, but I will work with Elon, of course.”

Altman co-founded OpenAI with Musk in 2015 but earlier this year Musk alleged in court that Altman, OpenAI, and the company’s president, Greg Brockman, unjustly enriched themselves and broke a founding contract. Musk’s claim was dismissed by a judge and jury.

OpenAI was hit by multiple safety crises over the summer, including when a swarm of its AI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website. Other agents accessed Australian government data. In the interview with Vanity Fair, Altman warned of “a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems” from rival open-source models. He suggested OpenAI could help its customers defend against the risk.

The company has scrapped the release of a cutting-edge model but Altman’s comments reflect a more bullish mood ahead of a stock market flotation.

The wave of public and political concern last month about the potentially catastrophic consequences of fast-progressing AI agents that act beyond human intent had led to hopes of US-wide or even international safety agreements.

However, Donald Trump and AI bosses including Altman and Dario Amodei of Anthropic signed a far more laissez-faire pact at the White House last week. The US president said he wanted the companies to “self-police” to limit the risks from AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons.

Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and Google DeepMind and as chief scientist at the UK’s AI Safety Institute, said warnings about AI risks understated the dangers.

“There’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems,” he said, adding that actions taken over the next two to 10 years would be decisive.

OpenAI’s David Robinson announced his departure at the weekend, saying “the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough” as they sprint from one product launch to the next.

His view was endorsed by Miles Brundage, an AI policy researcher who worked at OpenAI for six years. He said he regretted helping “spread the idea of iterative deployment”, which may have made sense when AI was less powerful “but makes no sense at all after many deaths have been tied to AI and as we’re careening towards extinction-level risks”.

fullText:
The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) dropped by almost 800,000 barrels last week, and the Trump administration moved forward with plans to sell another 40 million barrels in the coming months.

New data released on Monday by the US Department of Energy showed the US energy backstop sitting at 283 million barrels, down from 283.77 million the week prior.

That leaves about two weeks of US oil consumption in the reserve amid widespread worries about global stockpiles, which the head of Saudi Arabia's state producer on Monday called "scarily thin."

Amin Nasser, chief executive of Saudi Aramco, added at an Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday that releasing stockpiles will buy economies some time but won't fix the imbalances that have developed between supply and demand.

Yet these withdrawals in the US could soon accelerate after the Trump administration unveiled a request for bids from companies to buy up to 40 million barrels of crude oil from the SPR, with the aim of having the companies return those supplies "with additional premium barrels." The solicitation process is ongoing, and it's unclear if companies will agree to those terms.

The Trump administration continues to wrestle with high energy prices, less than a month before the midterm elections, and is reportedly preparing an executive order to expand access ‌to tax-exempt diesel, with the president confirming on Monday afternoon, "I'll be helping [farmers] with diesel."

In recent days, G7 countries — including the US — announced a new set of plans to release up to 100 million barrels of emergency fuel, including "a frontloaded substantial diesel release."

A White House official told Yahoo Finance that Trump intends to follow through on a commitment to release a total of 172 million barrels from the SPR, which was announced earlier this year.

The US energy backstop already sits at the lowest level seen since October of 1982, and a withdrawal of another 40 million barrels would put the reserve at its lowest level since records began being kept earlier in 1982, as the backstop was still coming online under President Ronald Reagan.

For his part, President Trump continues to project confidence that the US reserves will be quickly refilled. He told a crowd in Alabama over the weekend that, because of an energy deal with Venezuela, "we're going to be filling up very shortly our strategic reserves for nothing."

Experts say that, despite Trump's promises, refilling the reserves will be a complex and far-from-free process that could take years.

title: What we learned from Wales' Nations League window
description: On the back of a demanding four-game international window, BBC Sport Wales assesses the key talking points from Wales' Nations League A campaign so far.
fullText:
Craig Bellamy didn't waste his words when asked for his thoughts on Wales' opening four games of their return to the top tier of the Nations League.

It is hard to argue after a window that saw Wales lose three of their four fixtures, beaten in Portugal and Denmark and – following the lift of an eye-catching win over Norway – beaten again by the Danes.

That said, Wales' hopes of staying in League A – and the possibility of securing a Euro 2028 seedings boost – remains in their own hands going into next month's final pair of fixtures.

But what lessons can Wales take from the two-week test of their credentials?

In the immediate aftermath of the Denmark defeat, Bellamy had the new four-game window on his mind.

The former striker insisted the idea made "no sense" and suited the bigger nations, some of whom – such as Jurgen Klopp's Germany – named two squads for the four games.

Any hopes of extended time with the squad to make a coaching impact on the training pitch evaporated amid the reality of the travel and recovery between games.

And the fear that an untimely injury to a key player would see them miss four games rather than the two they would have previously was proven to have foundation when Harry Wilson and Joe Rodon were deemed unfit before a ball was kicked.

It would have been a problem in the past during the peaks of Gareth Bale and Aaron Ramsey and the like, but is even more so now.

Throw in the intensity with which Bellamy wants to play, and the drop off in energy was evident after a relatively promising start against Denmark.

"I felt we were a little bit flat, not as intense as we wanted it to be," reflected midfielder Jordan James. "That was expected after a really tough game the other day."

The issue goes beyond the pitch with a few too many empty seats on Sunday night's game for anyone's liking.

There was some hope among Football Association of Wales officials that the additional fixtures would create further momentum in the window, but the draining impact of cost and travel for fans seemingly took its toll – and will hit the revenue.

Wales' issue in all aspects is that they have no option but to get used to it.

Euro 2028 qualifying – and the chance of playing in a major tournament on home soil – will adopt the same format for games next September and October.

Bellamy bemoans new schedule after Denmark loss

Hojlund penalty condemns Wales to Denmark defeat

It has highlighted a problem for Bellamy that seems difficult to solve.

"I look at the players who came off the bench; Wes Burns plays in League One, Mark Harris plays in League One and Josh Sheehan has played for years in League One," summed up former Wales striker Iwan Roberts.

"That is the problem: when the starting 11 is not working, Craig Bellamy looks over his shoulder, and it's not nice to say, but he's looking at League One players to try to make the difference."

He added: "We just haven't got the strength in depth to make the impact that you need in games when we haven't got the players that were out injured in this international break."

Already without several key figures, David Brooks - who has not started a league game for Bournemouth this season - was also forced to withdraw midway through the camp due to injury to further limit Bellamy's options.

Fresh from his terrific display in which he netted Wales' opener and won the free kick for Neco Williams' stunning second, Dan James did not feature against the Danes on Sunday.

Kieffer Moore was also not introduced until late on with the score at 1-0 to Brian Riemer's side. It brings us nicely to the next point...

In the immediate aftermath of the defeat by Denmark, Roberts questioned: "I think questions have to be asked when we are chasing the game, when we did concede that goal with 15 minutes to go, why on earth he didn't bring Kieffer Moore on until 83 minutes? And he didn't bring Dan James on at all."

Prior to the match, Bellamy had confirmed James was not fit enough to start, although he had hoped the Leeds United winger would have been able to feature off the bench.

Ahead of the four-game window, Bellamy cited his desire for Wales to find "the next Harry Wilson" in the absence of the 29-year-old.

But many supporters were subsequently critical of the head coach's remark given that no new debuts were given during the international window while some others who have struggled to hit the desired heights for their country were given more opportunities.

No player has scored more Wales goals since Bellamy took charge than Harry Wilson.

His absence was sorely felt as Wales failed to score in three of their opening four League A matches.

It led to former Wales frontman John Hartson calling for more calm from other attackers such as Brennan Johnson, Kieffer Moore and Lewis Koumas.

"We are snatching at things. We need to slow it down a little, you've always got a bit more time," he told BBC Match of the Day Wales.

"We're playing at the highest level with lots of players at Championship level, but they have to find a way."

A fully-fit Wilson could be transformational for Bellamy and Wales as they bid to achieve their goal of avoiding relegation back into League B next month.

These four games were evidence of the new levels Ethan Ampadu has reached.

The Leeds skipper offered performances that simply highlighted his growing maturity. He made his mark on games in a way he might not have in the past and showed he is very much a player Wales can rely on.

"He does it every week, eight out of 10 every game," said former striker Sam Vokes.

"The crowd were singing his name at the end, he gives everything."

A "dream" player was how former striker Nathan Blake put it, while Robert Earnshaw suggested Wales can expect more going forward.

"There's more levels to him," he said. "Look at Harry Wilson last year – Ethan can do the same. There's more to come."

Denmark away was a pretty dismal night, but there were positives in Portugal.

And if Denmark at home felt a game too far, there was plenty to like about the Norway win that gives hope to cling to.

Especially given that, before this window, Wales had yet to win a game at this level of the Nations League.

Ultimately, when the disappointment lifts a little, Wales were beaten by single goals in two games – with the most recent via a penalty following an avoidable mistake.

"The quality's high which we expect," said Jordan James. "You get punished for little things, but I've also realised that you can play at this level. We've competed well and the last two games we've been well in them."

How much money do clubs get for Nations League players?

Haaland 'gave me his shirt... but didn't take mine'

The win over Norway – coupled with their defeat by Portugal on Sunday – means Wales are still third heading into the final games, courtesy of the head-to-head nature of this competition's tie-breakers.

Over the previous three Nations League campaigns combined, teams that finish bottom of a League A group have an average of 2.92 points after their six games.

Wales already have three points, and they still have to play Norway in Oslo and Portugal in Cardiff in November.

Before the current international camp even started, Bellamy spoke about targeting third place.

That would give Wales a chance of avoiding being relegated to League B and it would also improve their seeding for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw.

So what about teams who finish third in League A?

In the 2020-21, 2022-23 and 2024-25 campaigns combined, teams finishing third in League A groups have ended with an average of 6.42 points from six games.

It means Wales would realistically need one more win, or maybe two draws, to stand a chance of finishing third.

Even if they finish fourth, the tweak to the format means that only the two worst-ranked bottom sides go down automatically, with the other two heading into a play-off against a League B runner up.

With Serbia, Turkey and Czech Republic yet to register a point, they may already have done enough to line up a two-legged battle for survival in March, with Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ukraine, Scotland and Kosovo among the potential opponents.

title: Littler suffers defeat in World Youth Championships
description: Luke Littler is knocked out of the World Youth Championships in the semi-finals by Cam Crabtree.
fullText:
Luke Littler missed out on the chance to hold the senior and youth world titles simultaneously after suffering a surprise semi-final defeat at the World Youth Championship.

The 19-year-old world number one was beaten 6-5 by world number 68 Cam Crabtree, who will face German Jan Schmidt in the final on 29 November.

That match will take place on finals day at the Players Championship Finals in Minehead – an event Littler has also yet to qualify for having skipped the majority of Pro Tour events this season.

He is currently ranked 126th in the Players Championship order of merit and only the top 64 qualify.

Four Players Championship events remain, but two of those are in Den Bosch in the Netherlands - where Littler withdrew from events recently after being subjected to boos by the crowds.

Littler has won successive full World Championships and won the youth title as a 16-year-old in 2023, but the semi-final loss to 23-year-old Crabtree was his second successive exit at that stage having lost to Beau Greaves in 2025. He could though enter four more times, with the tournament open to players aged 23 or under at the start of the season.

The loss is the latest in a series of surprise exits for Littler, who was knocked out of the World Grand Prix in the first round by Luke Woodhouse and lost to Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals of the World Series of Darts finals.

title: Connor out, Lewis in as England name World Cup squad
description: Leeds Rhinos half-back Jake Connor is left out of England's Rugby League World Cup squad, with Hull KR's Mikey Lewis beating him to a place.
fullText:
Jake Connor missed out on a Rugby League World Cup spot by a "small margin" as England seek the players who can best stick to their gameplan, head coach Brian McDermott says.

Leeds Rhinos half-back Connor, the 2025 Super League Man of Steel, was left out of the 23-man squad for the tournament - to be held largely in Australia - with Hull KR's Mikey Lewis making the cut instead.

For Connor, it is another England disappointment to follow his controversial omission from the squad for last autumn's home series against Australia.

"Jake Connor missed out on selection by a small margin and it came down to who I think can best stick to the game plan and attack plan," McDermott said.

The 31-year-old had been expected to make the squad after being talked up by McDermott and enjoying a strong domestic season.

But Hull KR's Lewis, who endured an inconsistent year, has done enough to convince McDermott that he should join captain George Williams, the Warrington stand-off, and Wigan's Harry Smith as half-back options.

England begin their World Cup campaign against Tonga in Perth on 17 October, before facing France in the same city on 24 October and then Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on 30 October.

England squad: Matty Ashton (Warrington Wolves), AJ Brimson (Gold Coast Titans), Ben Currie (Warrington Wolves), Zach Eckersley (Wigan Warriors), Herbie Farnworth (Dolphins), Ethan Havard (Wigan Warriors), Max King (Bulldogs), Morgan Knowles (Dolphins), Mikey Lewis (Hull KR), Jez Litten (Hull KR), Junior Nsemba (Wigan Warriors), Brad O'Neill (Wigan Warriors), Kai Pearce-Paul (Wests Tigers), Victor Radley (Sydney Roosters), Hugo Savala (Sydney Roosters), Harry Smith (Wigan Warriors), Morgan Smithies (Canberra Raiders), Luke Thompson (Wigan Warriors), Sam Walters (Wigan Warriors), Ben Talty (Brisbane Broncos), Jack Welsby (St Helens), George Williams (Warrington Wolves), Dom Young (Newcastle Knights)

Australia-born Strange in England World Cup squad

Hawkins among five World Cup winners in England squad

There has been much debate about which half-backs would make the England squad after McDermott said last month that he would probably take three to the World Cup, and that captain Williams - who is heading to Australia to join NRL club Dolphins after the tournament - would be one of them.

McDermott said: "Jake has had a really good year. He had an outstanding year last year and got Man of Steel.

"What I've got is a squad full of players who I believe will best play to the game style, the attack plan or game model we identified many weeks ago, that I think we need to compete with the leading nations.

"We can't do the usual things, and I made this a point when I took the job. We've got to play with a point of difference.

"I've got a squad here who I believe are best suited to the attack plan and game model I think England need to play."

Explaining his decision to select Lewis, McDermott added: "I've picked a group of player that have recent history of playing in finals, winning finals, delivering when it matters.

"Mikey Lewis won a World Club Challenge at the start of this year and guided his team to a Challenge Cup final.

"I get he wasn't in the best of shape towards the back of the year and incurred a couple of bans but again, I'll just point people to the attack plan and game model I think England need to have to compete with the leading nations."

When he replaced Shaun Wane as head coach, McDermott indicated that he was keen to use heritage players - those who qualify for England through family background - to ensure the strongest possible squad.

He has called up two uncapped Australia-born players - versatile back Hugo Savala, part of Sydney Roosters' NRL Grand Final-winning squad, and Brisbane Broncos' front-rower Ben Talty.

Bulldogs prop Max King, born in Huddersfield while his Australian father David was a player there, also earns a first call-up. Victor Radley and AJ Brimson complete the Australia-born contingent in the squad.

Grand Final winners Wakefield have no players in the squad, with Tom Johnstone, Mike McMeeken, Caleb Hamlin-Uele and Jake Trueman all needing time to recover from injuries.

"It's a real shame that the Wakefield boys aren't available," McDermott said. "There's nothing we or they can do. They're all booked in for operations at the end of the year."

And also injured were Sydney Roosters centre Billy Smith - a scorer in Sunday's NRL Grand Final - Wigan centre Jake Wardle, Leeds winger Ash Handley and prop Mikolaj Oledzki, who is leaving Headingley to join NRL side Perth Bears.

Grand Finalists Warrington have three players in the squad - Matty Ashton and Ben Currie joining captain Williams - while Wigan have seven, including Man of Steel winner Brad O'Neill and uncapped centre Zach Eckersley.

Mikey Lewis over Jake Connor feels like a call made based on pace rather than any other metric, as the Hull KR half is much more of a runner than his opposite number.

He's also perhaps more of an off-the-bench spark than the Leeds playmaker, given George Williams and Harry Smith's blend of run threat and game management will probably get the nod at six and seven.

Herbie Farnworth has been one of the best players in the world for some time and has taken his game to new levels in 2026, and getting the centre involved must be among Brian McDermott's biggest tactical challenges.

Dom Young is another thoroughbred who England will look to out wide, having helped Newcastle to the NRL Grand Final.

Victor Radley's influence and savage tackling makes him a shoo-in for the pack, something that was missed in last year's Ashes series against Australia, and there are other big hitters in the ranks with Morgan Knowles and Morgan Smithies also sharpened by their NRL exploits, and Brad O'Neill back in the international picture after a Man of Steel year.

Staying with the pack, the prospect of a Kai Pearce-Paul and Junior Nsemba second-row pairing whets the appetite.

Elsewhere, the new imports from the NRL have pedigree; Max King has played State of Origin, Hugo Savala can jump into a number of backs spots and Ben Talty is an athletic front-rower who helped Brisbane to success in 2025.

Zach Eckersley has impressed for Wigan this year, and his strong build and athleticism - coupled with an ability to put a winger away - make him a solid inclusion, while Matty Ashton's return after his missed the Ashes with an anterior cruciate knee ligament injury gives England genuine pace out wide.

Everyone will have their opinion on the squad, which features no selections from Super League champions Wakefield - albeit with some contenders unavailable - but there is a balance to the selection.

McDermott has said England might need something different to truly test the best, and it is that conundrum which will again be at the forefront of his thoughts.

Reece Walsh has secured a place in Australia's men's World Cup squad, also named on Monday - although head coach Kevin Walters has refused to confirm whether he will be first-choice full-back.

Walsh has struggled to hit the heights of last season, when he inspired Brisbane Broncos to their first NRL Grand Final triumph in 19 years before helping Australia to a 3-0 Test series win over England.

He missed the end of this season to have ankle surgery, but with Penrith's Dylan Edwards ruled out of the World Cup with a knee injury, Walsh will vie for the full-back spot with James Tedesco - man of the match as Sydney Roosters beat Newcastle Knights 19-18 in Sunday's NRL Grand Final.

Loose forward Isaah Yeo will delay surgery on a torn pectoral muscle to captain Australia.

Winger Mark Nawaqanitawase - who scored two tries in Sydney's win on Sunday - is not in the squad because of his impending code switch to union with Japanese side Saitama Wild Knights. Second-row forward Angus Crichton is absent for the same reason, as he is joining NSW Waratahs.

Star half-back Nathan Cleary is out of the tournament with a broken ankle.

Dual-code winger Nawaqanitawase stars as Roosters win NRL Final

Ali Brigginshaw has missed out on the chance to go for a fourth World Cup winners' medal after being omitted from Australia's women's squad.

Head coach Jess Skinner said the 36-year-old Brisbane half-back - Australia's captain when they won the tournament in Manchester four years ago - was "upset" to be left out.

"That was one of the hardest phone calls I've had to make as a coach to a player and to talk about her and where she was," Skinner said.

title: How Evans defied history to become Britain's first world rally champion in 25 years
description: Elfyn Evans has been the nearly-man of world rally until he finally emulated the feats of Colin McRae and Richard Burns.
fullText:
For what must have felt like an eternity, Elfyn Evans feared history was repeating itself yet again.

At 3.05pm local time in Sardinia on Sunday, Evans could only stand and watch as another world rally title looked to be slipping from his grasp.

Evans was preparing in his head yet another runners-up speech - it would be his sixth - as he waited for Oliver Solberg to cross the finish line and be crowned world champion.

How could this be happening again?

Of the five previous times he had been championship runner-up, three had been decided on the final day and twice after he had taken a lead into the final event.

But at 3.06pm, for once the motor-racing gods were on his side.

With just two turns to go on the final stage of the final round and with victory in sight, Solberg somehow careered off the track into the Sardinian sand to hand Evans his first world title.

In the most dramatic of finishes, the 37-year-old from north Wales became the first British winner of the World Rally Championship (WRC) in 25 years.

Only two British men had taken the title since the WRC's 1977 inception, matching the exploits of legendary pair Colin McRae (1995) and Richard Burns (2001).

Louise Aitken-Walker was Britain's first world champion when WRC ran a women's version in 1990.

As it happened: Evans wins title as Solberg crashes on final stage

The five titles that got away as Evans seeks WRC glory

"It wouldn't by my proudest way of winning it, but it's job done," said Evans.

"It's been a difficult weekend. I felt on Friday things were slipping away. We were a bit powerless with the road position we had and Oliver was flying."

His experienced co-driver Scott Martin revealed Evans was already apologising for his stage performance as they waited for Solberg to finish.

"I've said all week that until we arrived at the beach after that last stage it was never over. How true that turned out to be," said Martin.

Evans and Martin have been consistent performers throughout the 2026 championship, through the streets of Monaco, the ice and snow of Sweden, the flowing roads of Chile, and the punishing, sun-baked gravel tracks of southern Europe.

Despite winning only two of the previous 12 events, the pair took a 21-point lead into the final race at Rally Italia Sardegna.

Solberg, whose father Petter won the 2003 title, was around one kilometre from glory only to suffer motorsport's version of Devon Loch.

"The lead up to this event gave us a bit of a buffer and we just about managed to hold on at the end. It was an incredible finish," said Evans.

"I feel for [Solberg] after he came so close and lost at the last moment. I've been in a similar situation and it will be tough for him for a few days, but he's shown he's one to watch for the future."

Evans, like Solberg, is also from fine rally-driving stock. His father Gwyndaf was British champion, as well as runner-up four times, but the motor dealer from farming stock never got the break to be a major contender on the world stage.

The curse of finishing second passed down to his son who had already turned professional by the time his father claimed the last of those near misses in 2010.

Evans clinched his first WRC stage win in Germany in 2014 and a first podium in Argentina a year later, before having to drop down to the WRC2 class in 2016.

Evans admitted that blow only fueled his determination to make it in the WRC and a first rally victory followed - in his home event in Wales - in 2017.

He has been remarkably consistent, finishing second for the title in 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024 and, perhaps most agonisingly, to Sebastien Ogier by just four points in the final race of 2025.

He appeared condemned to be one of sport's great runners-up until the late drama of Sardinia threw up one of the championship's most thrilling finishes.

There may have been a stroke of fortune about the title win, but few can deny Evans earned it.

title: A nation divided as Ronaldo left with big decision on Portugal future
description: BBC Sport looks at what could be the end of Cristiano Ronaldo's international career just days before the expected fanfare of Lionel Messi's Argentina goodbye.
fullText:
As Lionel Messi prepares to get a hero's farewell for his successful international career, Cristiano Ronaldo's could have ended with him running down the tunnel at the final whistle of a game he did not play.

After the World Cup, Argentina's Messi, 39, decided to retire from international football, while Ronaldo, 41, opted to play on for Portugal.

Yet there is the possibility that Messi's Argentina career will end up lasting a few days longer - with a home friendly with Benin on Tuesday marked as his final game.

Ronaldo, furious at being made to warm up and not be brought on against Norway in the Nations League, walked out on the Portugal squad after finding out he would not start against Denmark either.

The Al-Nassr forward has scored 146 goals and won 234 caps for Portugal - both world records.

After such a high-profile falling-out with new boss Jorge Jesus, also a larger than life character who does not back down, Ronaldo is facing a big decision.

Jesus has insisted he would be welcome back if he wants to return and talks between Ronaldo, his representatives and the Portuguese FA are ongoing as they look for a solution.

While Ronaldo could not carry on playing forever, this is not how he would have expected his international career to end.

His fans are remaining loyal to him, with social media full of posts supporting Ronaldo and criticising Jesus, while on the other side some fans and a lot of Portugal's media have been critical of what they see as selfish behaviour.

Ahead of Portugal's next match against Denmark in November lies a big decision for one of the world's greatest ever players.

Is this the end for Ronaldo - and would Portugal miss him?

It has all happened very quickly.

After the World Cup, Portugal replaced Roberto Martinez with Jesus, who had been Ronaldo's boss with Al-Nassr last season.

Less than two weeks ago, Ronaldo said: "I had a conversation with our president, with our coach. I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want."

Things were still looking OK when he started in the 1-0 win over Wales.

Jesus told Ronaldo he would be on the bench for the next game against Norway. After being told to warm up for a period of the game, he remained an unused substitute in a Portugal game for the first time in 18 years.

Guillem Balague, who wrote a book about Ronaldo in 2015, said: "He gets asked to warm up for the whole of the second half, practically.

"There are tacit rules in football: you don't do that to Pele, to Diego Maradona, to Lionel Messi, to Cristiano, right? That's what he's seen, that you don't do that to those kind of players."

And as the final whistle went he went down the tunnel instead of going to the fans with his team-mates.

Jesus said there was no falling out - but confirmed Ronaldo would not start the next game with Denmark either.

At that point Ronaldo left the training camp - and wrote on social media: "In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated."

Portugal's FA president Pedro Proenca flew to Copenhagen, landing at 02:30 in the morning, to try to smooth things over with Ronaldo but failed.

He has since said: "He is in the national team on sporting merit, and that must be unquestionable. We have to pay tribute to Ronaldo."

After beating Norway on Sunday in their final Nations League match - again without Ronaldo - Jesus said: "If he wants to, he'll return to the national team. We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who's going to decide.

"He's the one who should decide how he wants to end his time with the national team."

On several billboards in Lisbon posters went up praising Ronaldo and criticising Jesus.

They read, in Portuguese: "Thank you Cristiano Ronaldo for everything you did for Portugal. You will always be our captain.

"Jorge Jesus was not up to the task. Lack of sensitivity. Treating a captain wrongly. Inflated ego."

One was placed next to the Estadio da Luz, home of Benfica - who Jesus managed to three league titles.

At the Denmark game, some fans wore T-shirts spelling out 'Love you Jesus' while others were head-to-toe in Ronaldo merch.

Denmark striker Rasmus Hojlund, incidentally, celebrated his goal with his idol Ronaldo's trademark 'siuuu' - something he has done previously when netting against Portugal.

Portugal's newspapers had differing perspectives.

Record - who the forward owns shares in - said "Ronaldo leaves after clash with Jesus" and Jornal de Noticias said it was "the end of a historic era".

"A sad goodbye," said Bola, while Jogo went for "CR7 turns his back on the national team".

Meanwhile, videos were posted online of angry fans ripping up their Portugal jerseys.

Jesus and Proenca were booed leaving a building in Copenhagen.

But many foreign fans purely supported Portugal because of Ronaldo - so they do not necessarily represent the views of actual Portuguese supporters.

Portugal fan Maria Ribeiro, from Lisbon, said: "It is so hard for all us fans. We all love him but it is getting too much now. It is hard to imagine Portugal without Ronaldo but maybe this is the time. There is too much arguing between ourselves."

Ronaldo's World Cup career ends in tears as 'pandering' Martinez departs

Ronaldo's search for a record 1,000 career goals remains on but will he have to finish that at club level in Saudi Arabia?

He has scored 979 times for Portugal, Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus and Al-Nassr.

While his old rival Messi scored eight goals, and assisted four more, to take Argentina to the summer World Cup final - Portugal fell at the last-16 stage.

Ronaldo scored three goals in the tournament but failed to have an impact in their loss to Spain, leading BBC pundit Chris Sutton to say he was "waddling around the pitch like a grandad".

Ronaldo's former United team-mate Wayne Rooney added: "He is a genius, a superstar. What he has given to football and millions of people is something very rare.

"He will be disappointed because he believed he could win this tournament. But time gets us all. It's a sad day for football."

In the last nine years of Ronaldo's international career, Portugal's win percentage without him is slightly better - 64% to 63% - and they have scored 2.7 goals a game without him compared to 2.1 with him.

The two biggest wins in their history - 9-0 over Luxembourg and 9-1 against Armenia - came in the last two qualifying matches that he missed, both through suspension.

Journalist Marcus Alves, who covers Portugal, said: "How much gratitude is enough? That's a question that Portuguese fans have been asking for a few years now.

"The whole soap opera that seems to follow the mere presence of the 41-year-old striker got to a point where patience was running out.

"Of Portugal's last five coaches, Ronaldo had issues with four of them – Carlos Queiroz, Paulo Bento, Fernando Santos and now Jesus. That's too much distraction when Portugal have arguably their best generation ever."

Portugal boss says door open for Ronaldo return

title: Sam Altman: ‘The world should accept some bad things happening’ for benefits of AI
description:

fullText:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman admits "something's clearly not working" with the artificial intelligence money that has flooded the midterm elections — and he doesn't expect President Donald Trump's rebrand of the technology to improve his industry's image with the American public, either.

"I get why AI has a really negative perception right now," Altman told Brendan Bordelon in an exclusive interview marking the launch of Decoded by POLITICO. "I don't think spending money on politics is what's going to make people feel better about it. The industry needs to figure out a way to address what the actual concerns are, and right now, a lot of people in the industry are being quite tone deaf."

In the wide-ranging conversation, Altman offered a window into how OpenAI is confronting new political pressures and intensified competition with Anthropic, its corporate archrival run by former employee Dario Amodei.

Altman says OpenAI is more tolerant than Anthropic of less-than-catastrophic harms from AI, drawing out what he sees as a fundamental split in worldview between the two leading labs even as they converge on tougher rules in the wake of high-profile autonomous hacking incidents.

"We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency," said Altman, who characterized those harms as linked to "the lighter touch regulatory stance that we advocate for."

"I wouldn't take a trade of saying like, 'We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no kind of like misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen,'" said Altman. "Because I think people will do tremendously orders of magnitude more good stuff."

The OpenAI head also suggested there needs to be a new "liability framework" for companies whose models are capable of autonomous cyberattacks, like the Hugging Face hack over the summer and incidents involving government websites. Altman called that behavior "clearly unacceptable," and said that "if something goes wrong with our models during training, there's going to be some version of that we need to be responsible for."

"This is the kind of thing that we are hoping our policymakers will all debate," he added, as Congress remains deadlocked.

And while Altman defended a "morally binding" AI safety accord that Trump signed with tech CEOs last week as a great start for the industry, he predicted calls for guardrails will continue and said he would "welcome something more." He also said he shares the concerns of those who worry AI rules are being crafted by the White House and tech executives without input from Congress or the public.

"If we do too much to restrict this technology in the name of safety, and we end up with a small number of companies or people — or perhaps one country — that have too much power over this, that also is a way that this can go horribly wrong," Altman said.

Trump paired last week's AI agreement with an executive order renaming artificial intelligence to "super intelligence." It's a term Altman considers more accurate, though he doubts the public will find it "less scary." He expects people to keep using "AI" — and unlike Elon Musk, he won't be renaming OpenAI to OpenSI. "Brands are sticky," Altman said.

Throughout the interview, Altman sought to explain his company's new policy posture. He recently agreed with Amodei on the need to slow down AI's development, and his lobbyists have increasingly followed Anthropic in backing new safety requirements at all levels of government.

But despite emphasizing "a lot of daylight" between OpenAI and Anthropic, Altman also tried to distance himself — on both policy and politics — from the Silicon Valley investors who are spending heavily to block strict regulations, including through the pro-AI super PAC network Leading the Future.

"When it comes to the potential of a serious loss of control to AI … this is where I would say to the accelerationists, let's be a little thoughtful about lurching into this future," he said, using a descriptor often applied to the tech leaders and advisers who have Trump's ear on AI.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman has pulled away from those donors as well, reportedly backing out of a second $25 million donation to LTF and apologizing to employees internally for creating a "distraction." (Altman said he hadn't seen The New York Times report when asked if he agreed that the money was counterproductive, and that LTF never approached him for money.)

From the AI race with China to his favorite world leader and why the ChatGPT maker hasn't made all of its hacks public, Altman went deeper with Decoded than we've heard him go before.

Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.

Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.

It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.

A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.

Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.

Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.

"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.

Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades. It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.

CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.

The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.

CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.

Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.

The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.

"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.

The complaint claims  Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.

Holt's affidavit claims  Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.

She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.

On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.

Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.

Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.

Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA, Taiwan's national news agency.

Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.

Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang, 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.

Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.

The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.

New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.

In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.

title: Bellamy bemoans new schedule after Denmark loss
description: Craig Bellamy suggests the new four-match international window has counted against Wales after Sunday's Nations League defeat against Denmark.
fullText:
Craig Bellamy suggested the new four-match international window had counted against Wales after Sunday's Nations League defeat against Denmark.

His side failed to build on Thursday's win over Norway as they were deservedly beaten thanks to a second-half Rasmus Hojlund penalty.

It was a third loss in four games played inside 10 days as part of the newly elongated international break.

Head coach Bellamy said his injury-hit squad paid the price for the heavy workload he feels benefits the bigger nations and "puts a real stress" on countries like Wales.

"Physically, I completely agree with the ones who don't like [the new window]. It makes no sense," he added.

"Four games at this type of level… for the other nations, we know who they are because I was in the room when they all voted for it.

"I was one of the ones who wasn't [voting for it], because we know it's a complete disadvantage to us."

Traditionally, international sides have played six games across three windows - all of which have featured two fixtures - in September, October and November.

But for the first time this year, the September and October breaks were merged.

Wales' hopes of coping with the new schedule were not helped by a string of injuries, with stars such as Karl Darlow, Joe Rodon, Dylan Lawlor and Harry Wilson missing the entire camp and David Brooks dropping out of the squad after defeat by Portugal in the opening game.

Bellamy said Dan James was not fit enough to play against Denmark after he was left on the bench at the Cardiff City Stadium, and acknowledged Ben Davies probably should have been rested after he was withdrawn late on.

"If we have a few injuries, which we had more than one or two, they miss four games," said Bellamy.

"We can deal with two, do you understand? And then the squad will get really tested. The intensity of the squad, the athleticism, really I think [the four-game break] is designed for the elites.

"[They can] say, we can go, we can go, we can turn over these games really, really quickly and we can change, we can change [the team] like for like because we have the numbers. So, it puts a real stress on a lot of us."

Wales rarely looked like scoring against Denmark, who came close to breaking the deadlock on a couple of occasions before Hjolund's 75th-minute winner.

"On Thursday [against Norway] we were on the front foot so we're able to shorten distance," Bellamy added.

"Today, we just couldn't work it well enough, couldn't get the energy up enough to be able to have a bigger say in the game."

Danny Ward made fine saves from Hojlund and Gustav Isaksen to keep Wales level but it was the goalkeeper's error, and foul, which led to the penalty.

Bellamy, though, suggested the game had not swung on Ward's mistake, adding: "Obviously it's the decisive moment, but he made two incredible saves before that.

"I thought Denmark with the physicality were able to just crank it a little bit. You see their runs are really menacing, so I felt they were knocking on the door. He did incredibly well to keep it 0-0 to that time."

Despite defeat, Wales climbed to third in Nations League Group A4 courtesy of their head-to-head record against Norway after the Norwegians were beaten 2-1 in Portugal.

Wales play Norway in Oslo next month before completing the campaign with a home game against Portugal three days later.

title: Humphries wins Grand Prix to end barren spell
description: World number two Luke Humphries ends a 16-month wait for a PDC major trophy with a stunning 6-4 victory over Gerwyn Price in the World Grand Prix final.
fullText:
World number two Luke Humphries ended a 16-month wait for a PDC major trophy with a stunning 6-4 victory over Gerwyn Price in the World Grand Prix final.

Humphries, 31, was at the top of the sport two years ago but has found his dominance superseded by Luke Littler and had failed to taste major success since winning the Premier League in May 2025.

A ranking title had eluded him since claiming the Masters in February last year, but he showed his class and an abundance of character to lift the title at the unique 'double-in, double-out' tournament in Leicester.

The second seed, who was in a record-breaking fourth successive World Grand Prix final, trailed Price 3-0 but won four sets on the spin to take control.

Price levelled but Humphries broke in the deciding leg of set five and then won three straight legs to be crowned champion.

It is his second World Grand Prix title, adding to his 2023 success that started his march to becoming world number one.

The victory ensures he retains his number two ranking from the Netherlands' Gian van Veen.

"It's kind of like I needed this to give me a bit of confidence," Humphries told Sky Sports.

"It's been a torrid 15 or 18 months, losing so many major finals. I felt like I had not much to give tonight."

Defeat for Price means his four-year wait for a major PDC title continues, while he has now lost five successive major finals, including three this year.

World Grand Prix: Brilliant Humphries fights back to beat Price - as it happened

Darts' World Grand Prix: Results and prize money

Price, who was playing in a fourth Grand Prix final, claimed the first set with a stunning 132 three-dart average.

He raced into a 3-0 lead and Humphries admitted afterwards that avoiding a 6-0 clean sweep was on his mind such was the brutality that Price was producing.

The fourth set saw the momentum swing however. With Price waiting on tops to move to within two sets of victory, Humphries nicked it by taking out a brilliant 105, with what he said "felt like the biggest shot of my career".

From there his levels started to rise and he claimed the following three sets to lead.

Price rallied in set eight and won three successive legs to force a best-of-three finale, but, after a short break, Humphries found another gear.

Set nine went to a deciding leg, but unlike the previous four sets in the match where that had happened, there was a break of throw, with Humphries finishing in 10 darts.

That left Price dejected and Humphries won three unanswered legs to claim a ninth major PDC title.

"The sport is in such a special place that when you pick these trophies up they mean a lot more," said Humphries.

"When I was winning, I don't think there were so many good players. I'm happy to win a couple a year - one a year is great.

"To go on and win like I did is going to be tough. I don't think I can't do it, I'm just trying to pick up as many titles as I can.

"I worked incredibly hard, showed a lot of grit and determination. I think these are a lot sweeter than the ones you win with ease."

title: How Sullivan, Hall Have Turned Heads With U.S. Men’s National Team
description: Two teenagers - Cavan Sullivan and Julian Hall - continued to stand out for the U.S. Men's National Team in its 3-0 victory over Mexico in an international friendly on Saturday night.
fullText:
Three games into Mauricio Pochettino's second tenure as U.S. Men's National Team head coach, life could not be much better for the side.

The Americans have won three consecutive matches.

Their success with a 4-1 victory over Peru on Sept. 26. It continued with a 4-2 win past Chile. And then it hit a high note with a resounding 3-0 triumph over archrival Mexico on Saturday, Oct. 3. The USA hosts Canada in the final match of their rare four-game friendlies in St. Paul, Minn., on Tuesday night.

Beyond the impressive results have been the performances of several teenagers who have gotten their collective feet wet in international soccer.

Two teens produced some history at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Ariz.

Forward Julian Hall, 18, scored to give the U.S. a 1-0 first-half lead against the Mexicans. The New York Red Bulls forward became the third player in USMNT history to score in his first three appearances. He also became the youngest player to accomplish that feat.

Midfielder Cavan Sullivan, 17, became the youngest player to score for the men's national side in the final half, five days after celebrating his 17th birthday on Sept. 28.

"I think it's a fantastic problem for us," Pochettino was quoted by ESPN.com about his young players. "I think we will take the right decision in the right moment, but I think it's a very good problem to see.

"Now it's not a moment at all, but yes, we appreciate that situation and of course hope that we will be in that situation that young players perform in the way that they deserve to be with us."

Why USMNT Coach Pochettino Is Doing Some Forward Thinking

Sullivan, named Major League Soccer's Player of the Month for September, has been highly touted as the next big thing on the national team. The Philadelphia Union midfielder's overall play with the USMNT was impressive in these matches, but he didn't score a goal. He remedied that in the 63rd minute.

He intercepted a horrible clearance by Mexican goalkeeper Raul Rangel before lofting an uncontested 34-yard shot into the net for a two-goal lead. Teammate Mathis Albert, who scored earlier in the week, held the record at 17 years and 131 days.

"I remember pressing the goalie," Sullivan told TNT Sports. "I remember I probably shouldn't press the goalie. It felt like there was not really anybody pressing behind me. But that's why you put the work in, and I was rewarded for doing so. From there, it was sort of a blackout. I just remember chipping the ball, hoping it didn't hit the crossbar or go over. I kid you not. I was getting nervous when it was in the air. And then, t's a blur. Knee slide. My knees hurt. I'm really happy that the guys ran down and celebrated with me."

Why USMNT Coach Pochettino Decided On A Fresh Start With Youngsters

Pochettino loved what he had seen.

"I think he's a talented player with enormous quality, but with a very good balance, in possession and out of possession," Pochettino said, according to ESPN.com. "He's a fighter, he's a warrior. It's difficult to find this type of player with a tremendous quality.

"And then I think Cavan showed in possession with the ball on the field [and] when he need to be chasing people and recover the ball. That is my impression after maybe three weeks together. And that is unbelievable, to have a player like this. I think it's a fantastic news for USA. Hope that continues in that way."

Hall, who bolted off to a quick start with the Red Bulls by scoring nine goals before the 2026 FIFA World Cup break, went into a personal 12-game scoreless streak. He recently rediscovered his scoring touch in Major League Soccer and has continued it with the national team.

On Saturday night, the Manhattan, N.Y. native continued his scoring onslaught to give the hosts the lead in the 28th minute.

Gio Reyna beat his man down the right flank. Just as he was about to run over the end line, Reyna sent the ball toward the net. Goalkeeper Raul Rangel, who produced four clean sheets in the World Cup, could not handle it. An alert Hall made El Tri pay by tapping the ball into the net from point-blank range.

"I mean, three goals in three games is not bad for a striker, especially in your first three games in the national team," Reyna was quoted by FoxSports.com. "He sort of has that eye for goal."

After he did damage against Chile on Tuesday, Hall talked about his experience.

"It's been amazing to share the field with some amazing players," Hall said on the TNT post-game show. "They put me in the right spots, and I'm just doing as much as I can to put them away."

Hall praised Red Bulls head coach Michael Bradley for helping him and USMNT and club teammate, 17-year-old midfielder Adri Mehmeti, for their development this MLS season.

"It's been amazing," he said. "We have a lot of young guys on our team, including Adri. He's helped us so much in our development. He's a big reason as to why me and him are here right now. So, he's been amazing. He gave us amazing advice before we got here, and he's been awesome."

Vozinha's Amazing Legend Keeps Growing With Yashin Nomination

After the win over Mexico, Pochettino talked about not rushing the burgeoning stars of the next generation of USMNT players.

But Hall's performances might open the door for him to be a part of the U.S. squad when it plays a home-and-home series in the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals in November.

"It's a fantastic problem for us," Pochettino told FoxSports.com's Doug McIntyre when he asked if the performances of Hall and the other youngsters might alter their plans.

Most national team coaches live for "problems" like that.

title: World No. 979 Stewart's dilemma after finishing fourth at Alfred Dunhill Links
description: Scotland's Michael Stewart has a choice to make after securing his best finish at a DP World Tour event.

On Wednesday, Michael Stewart earned £2,500 for finishing runner-up in the Tartan Pro Tour event at Duddingston Golf Club near Edinburgh.

Four days later, the world number 979 has just picked up nearly 100 times that by finishing joint fourth behind winner Adrian Meronk at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship.

But what the 36-year-old Scot regards as "without doubt" the best week of his career has left him with a dilemma.

Finishing in the top 10 - two shots behind Poland's Meronk, one behind Denmark's Niklas Norgaard and South Africa's Casey Jarvis, and tied with England's Tommy Fleetwood - means he qualifies for next week's big-money Spanish Open.

However, that clashes with the conclusion to the Tartan Pro Tour, the Gleneagles Masters, after which Stewart will qualify for next year's second-tier Challenge Tour should he protect his current second place.

"Right now, in all honesty, in my mind, it's definitely play the Tartan Pro Tour final at Gleneagles," Stewart said.

"If I don't go and somebody overtakes me, I don't think that's the right thing to do.

"I've played so well to put myself in that position as well. There's so many good players behind me. One of three or four guys can catch me and, if one of them plays well, they can win.

"It would be silly if I wasn't to go to Gleneagles and at least tee it up and try and secure my Challenge Tour card.

"That was my goal at the start of the year."

While Meronk was earning his fifth win on the DP World Tour, Stewart, who finished one stroke ahead of compatriot and defending champion Robert MacIntyre, was making only his sixth appearance - having missed the cut in his previous five events.

The Ayrshire-based former Walker Cup player finished joint 52nd at The Open Championship at Royal Liverpool in 2023 but described his performance at Kingsbarns, Carnoustie and St Andrews this week as a career highlight.

"The Open was amazing, but I felt really disheartened after the Sunday at The Open because I felt like I threw away what could have been a really special weekend," he said.

"But this is amazing. It gives yourself a little bit more belief that you can go on and compete at this level."

MacIntyre was delighted to see his fellow Scot's hard work rewarded.

"It's brilliant," he said. "That's exactly what I was hoping for.

"When we spoke at Kingsbarns when he had a good second round, it was like, hopefully he can do something special that gives him a chance.

"I play the odd game of golf with him and his short game is superb."

title: Harry Kane moves into tie for 7th place on all-time international scorers list
description: The Bayern Munich and England striker is an incredible goalscorer.
fullText:
Harry Kane has added another remarkable milestone to an international career that is already loaded with them.

The England captain has moved into seventh place on the all-time international goalscoring list, reaching 89 goals for the Three Lions. Kane is now level with Malaysia legend Mokhtar Dahari and sits within striking distance of another Bayern Munich legend, Robert Lewandowski, who has 92 goals.

Kane is now alongside some of the greatest international goalscorers the sport has ever produced. The list is topped by Cristiano Ronaldo with 146 goals, followed by Lionel Messi (125), Iran's Ali Daei (108), India's Sunil Chhetri (95), Belgium's Romelu Lukaku (94), and Lewandowski (92).

Harry Kane now has 89 goals for England, putting him in 7th place in the all-time list of international top scorers pic.twitter.com/fzlUMhiHpM

At 33 years old, the Bayern Munich striker has already established himself as England's all-time leading scorer, and his continued international output means the players immediately ahead of him are firmly within reach.

Lukaku is only five goals ahead, Chhetri is six ahead, and Lewandowski is just three ahead.

That makes his climb up the leaderboard particularly compelling. Kane could realistically pass several legends before his England career comes to an end, even if Cristiano Ronaldo's record remains in another realm entirely.

For Bayern Munich fans, there is another reason to appreciate this milestone. Kane's goalscoring feats for England place him in the same historical conversation as Lewandowski — and Kane still has plenty of football left to play.

Knowing Harry Kane, he likely already has the next milestone in his sights.
