fullText:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Friday that a woman who alleges she was drugged and raped by multiple members of a Cornell University fraternity in 2024 was "failed" by those obligated to protect her.

Hochul's comments came a day after announcing she had lost faith in the district attorney overseeing the Cornell University rape case and signed an executive order appointing New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to lead the investigation.

"In what world would the police learn from a victim that she'd been literally gang raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?" Hochul said at a press conference with James in New York. "In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved or even request the full transcript?

"At every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her," Hochul said.

James said that the case is "now an active criminal investigation."

"We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions," James said, adding: "I know that you want answers. I do too."

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has come under intense scrutiny in recent days over his decision not to prosecute anyone when the initial allegations were made in 2024.

In a civil lawsuit filed last month against the school and seven current and former fraternity members, a former student identified as "Jane Doe" alleged that she was the victim of a "gang rape" at the Chi Phi fraternity on Cornell's Ithaca, N.Y., campus on Oct. 19, 2024. She said she was already intoxicated when she arrived and was given ketamine before and during the alleged assault. She reported the incident to campus police three weeks later.

Van Houten said earlier this week that Jane Doe's sworn statement to police didn't include allegations that she was "drugged against her will or gang raped."

"On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual," Van Houten said. "My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later."

On Tuesday, CBS New York published excerpts from Jane Doe's Nov. 14, 2024, interview with Cornell police, in which she asserted, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."

"Shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors," Hochul said Friday.

Van Houten said he was not provided with a transcript of her interview before his office decided not to pursue charges.

"I'm going to follow up on this because this is news to me," Van Houten told CBS. "If she had said those words, we certainly would want to have explored that more. Like I said, that wasn't provided to me."

According to ABC News, Jane Doe told the school's investigators that she "felt like bait" on the night of the alleged assault.

"I felt like lions around me," she said during a 2025 hearing. "It just was a totally debilitating place to be in."

The comments were included in a 99-page report prepared by the university as part of its Title IX investigation, per ABC.

The report also included comments from a fraternity member who Cornell's investigation concluded did not engage in the assault but was found responsible for "attempted sexual exploitation."

"I was sorry that maybe if it wasn't consensual and she was victimized, I was sorry for not stopping it," the fraternity members said, according to ABC.

Two of the men have released statements through their lawyers denying they participated in a sexual assault, according to the Associated Press.

Cornell University issued a statement pushing back against claims that the school did not thoroughly punish those involved in the alleged assault.

"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," the university said. "A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault."

Hochul announced on Wednesday that Cornell had agreed to initiate an independent review of its initial response to the allegations.

The governor also said she would work to close a loophole in New York law, which states that someone who was voluntarily intoxicated cannot claim they were mentally incapacitated during an assault, unless they can show they were "physically helpless" and unable to communicate consent.

"If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol," Hochul said. "Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period."

On Sept. 14, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell University and seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, alleging that she was the victim of a "gang rape" at the fraternity house when she was incapable of consent — and that the school failed to protect her from "sexual predators" on its campus.

The defendants named in the lawsuit include Cornell, the seven fraternity members, the Chi Phi fraternity, the woman's own sorority, Delta Delta Delta, and an off-campus bar that allegedly served her alcohol.

She is seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages resulting from "sustained psychological injuries, severe emotional distress, along with pain and suffering and loss of enjoyment of life."

According to her lawsuit, Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the school in October 2024 when she went to visit a friend at the fraternity house on Cornell's Ithaca, N.Y., campus while intoxicated. Shortly after arriving, Jane Doe alleged that she was pressured by two fraternity brothers into snorting what they said was ketamine before sexually assaulting her. One of the men then allegedly sent a message to the fraternity's Snapchat group suggesting that she was available for sex. A screengrab of part of the chat was included in the lawsuit.

According to the complaint, multiple other members of the fraternity showed up, and she was raped for hours.

"The Snapchat was disgusting and vulgar and immoral," Van Houten told ABC News. "But the question that we analyzed was, did Jane Doe consent to what happened? And the law in New York state is clear: That if you are voluntarily intoxicated, or under the influence of drugs such that your judgment is impaired, that does not legally under the penal law constitute your inability to consent."

During the alleged assault, the fraternity members "began pouring lines of Ketamine all over her body and snorting them," according to the complaint.

"At around 5:45 AM, this assault concluded and Plaintiff lost consciousness," the lawsuit stated.

About three weeks later, on Nov. 8, 2024, Jane Doe reported the incident to the university's police department.

According to ABC News, Jane Doe told police in a sworn statement on Nov. 15, 2024, that the incident "felt like coercion," and that at one point she said "no to the foursome" one of the fraternity brothers had proposed. She also stated: "I felt like I was unable to make any decision because of how intoxicated I was."

According to the New York Times, she told Cornell's Title IX investigators that she did not consider herself a victim until she saw the incident being discussed in an online forum.

"Are Chi Phi brothers Crips or Bloods because I hear they have been doing hell Gang Banging?" one user wrote.

"They do drugs and gang r*ped a sophomore," wrote another.

"That's the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn't a whore and that I was assaulted," Jane Doe told investigators, per the Times.

One of the accused men's lawyers told NBC that his client "made an immature comment on Snapchat," but "did nothing else."

Cornell's months-long Title IX investigation included at least 12 hearings, according to the lawsuit, which said that the accused fraternity members were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell."

Two of the seven accused fraternity members were ultimately expelled, while the others received lesser sanctions, according to the complaint. Jane Doe dropped out of school.

According to CBS, two were suspended for at least two semesters. Cornell denies that students only had to write essays as a disciplinary measure.

Last week, Cornell issued a statement saying that it had concluded its Title IX investigation but would not disclose individual sanctions, citing federal privacy laws.

"The Cornell Office of Civil Rights and the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies. The Xi chapter of Chi Phi fraternity remains barred from our campus," the statement said: "Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students and we therefore are unable to make a public statement on any other disciplinary response. Violations of university policies could lead to sanctions up to and including suspension or expulsion. We will respond in detail through the legal process."

The university also pointed out that it launched a task force on campus sexual assault in the wake of the incident and issued a report in March with recommendations for "an environment that fosters sexual health and safety."

"Several of the recommendations have already been implemented, while others are in development with oversight by a university implementation committee," Cornell said.

According to USA Today, more than 1,200 incidents of sexual assault, domestic and dating violence and stalking were reported to Cornell University's Title IX from 2018 through 2024. Of those, 14 cases resulted in suspensions, while seven ended in expulsion or dismissal, per the paper.

"Cornell takes each report seriously and, to the greatest extent possible, honors a complainant's decision not to pursue resolution," Rebecca Valli, a Cornell spokesperson, said in a statement to USA Today. "The university provides support and resources regardless of whether the respondent is subject to our conduct processes, and regardless of whether a complainant consents to an investigation."

The harrowing allegations revealed in Jane Doe's lawsuit prompted reactions from several celebrities, including Florence Pugh, who posted a lengthy response on Instagram calling for men to speak out against sexual violence.

"This is really the moment where we need our men to be as horrified and as sickened as us," Pugh wrote. "You need to be leading conversations about how we change the allowance and complicity of this behaviour as much as we are. How can you expect us to trust that it's 'not all men' when in moments like this, many of you stay quiet?"

In an expletive-laden Instagram post, actor Josh Gad tore into Cornell, seizing on allegations in the civil lawsuit that the fraternity members were required to write essays as part of the adjudication process.

"When we start setting a precedent that our girls and women can be brutally raped, and the resulting disciplinary action is to hand out (checks notes) ESSAYS (like it's Bart Simpson being a lil' rascal), about why it was wrong to brutally violate an innocent girl, we have lost our f***ing minds," Gad wrote.

Toby Morton, a former South Park writer, launched a website, TheCornell7.org, dedicated to holding the school and the accused fraternity members accountable.

"Accountability is coming," Morton wrote on Instagram.

Mariska Hargitay posted a joint statement on Instagram with the Joyful Heart Foundation, which supports survivors of sexual assault, domestic violence, and child abuse, with a quote from a scathing editorial by the Cornell Daily Sun.

"Arrest them," Heated Rivalry star Hudson Williams wrote in an Instagram story while sharing a photo of the seven accused men, according to Variety.

"F*** them and f*** Cornell, too!" he added.

At a town hall in Ithaca, N.Y., earlier this week, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat, said that "the culture of rape, sexual assault and pedophilia is protected in elite institutions across the United States, including Cornell."

Ocasio-Cortez recalled her own experience as a freshman at Boston University.

"Within maybe 10 seconds of me walking into a party — at a gym, at a school facility — someone had touched me inappropriately," Ocasio-Cortez said.

"Jane Doe, that survivor, lost her education because you can't stay in school when something like that happens to you," Ocasio-Cortez told the crowd. "She had to lose her education, and those men were protected by an institution and granted an Ivy League degree as a reward. Never again."

The congresswoman said she had a message to Jane Doe and other survivors of sexual assault.

"I want you to know that you are not defined by the things that have happened to you," Ocasio-Cortez said. "You are bigger than that. You are stronger than them. And they will never define you for your entire life. And that you can achieve anything that you want to achieve, from one survivor to another."

fullText:
Officials say it will be a staging facility for people who are self-deporting.

A new facility in Alexandria, Louisiana, may begin receiving undocumented families with children, local officials and immigrant rights advocates say.

The 528-bed facility will house families with children, unaccompanied minors, and single adult females as they await removal inside renovated former Air Force barracks at England Airpark, a former military base that now houses the Alexandria International Airport and an immigration detention facility, according to a draft agreement between ICE and the England Economic and Industrial Development District (EEIDD) reviewed by ABC News.

A communications manager for EEIDD told ABC News the facility could start receiving people "within the next week or two."

The facility would be the second constructed to house children since President Donald Trump's second term began but is the first to hold unaccompanied minors who are usually held in shelters under the custody of the Department of Health and Human Services before deportation or release.

A board of commissioners that governs the airpark approved the facility in February amid protests from local residents.

The facility will be managed by LaSalle Family Foundation, a nonprofit arm of LaSalle Corrections, a private prison company that manages several immigration detention centers across the country. Daily operations will be run by Anovaeon, which describes itself as a humanitarian response company. The operators are calling the facility the Alexandria Family Staging Center and say it will house people who are voluntarily self-deporting or voluntarily leaving the country, for an average stay of under 48 hours.

Last week, Robert Hagen, the project manager for LaSalle Family Foundation told commissioners the facility was 95% completed.

During board meetings that have at times become contentious with police having to remove opponents of the plans, operators of the facility have attempted to push back against the notion that it's a detention center.

"This project right over here is not a detention center, it's a staging center for families who are voluntarily departing this country, admittedly through pretty crappy circumstances on their end. I acknowledge that," Anovaeon CEO Eric Fritz said at a commissioner board meeting last week.

Fritz said the facility will provide medical care, mental health care, "quality meals," soccer fields and free international calling, among other resources.

A pamphlet distributed during one of the board meetings and obtained by ABC News said migrant families will be held in a "non-detained" setting at the facility. However, during last week's board meeting, Anovaeon Senior Director of Operations Jeffrey Lynch acknowledged operators would have to alert ICE if someone attempted to leave the facility.

"I think what we would do is, we would approach the individual, say 'Look, you're part of this program. It's in your best interest to follow through with the program,'" Lynch said. "If they were adamant about it, I think we would open the gate but at the same time we would be in communication with ICE, letting them know what's happening."

There's an ICE office "literally steps away" from the facility, Lynch added.

"They're literally steps away and they would be there to either intervene, convince them to come back in, or take whatever steps they would take as part of their case management practices," Lynch said.

A draft of the Intergovernmental Service Agreement between DHS and the EEIDD obtained by the advocacy group National Immigration Project and reviewed by ABC News said one of the purposes of the agreement is to provide "ICE alien detention in a secure environment under the authority of the Immigration and Nationality Act."

A communications manager for the EEIDD said she could not share the final agreement with ABC News, noting that ICE had to sign off before it could be shared.

At a press conference on Wednesday, immigrant rights groups and attorneys denounced the facility and raised concerns that the property was contaminated with PFAS.

"There can be no hiding what this is, this is a detention center. People are not free to leave," said Stephanie Alvarez-Jones, Southeast Regional Attorney for the National Immigration Project.

DHS, EEIDD and Anovaeon did not respond when asked to address concerns about possible contamination, or whether people would be restrained at any point during their stay or during removal.

DHS did not provide an estimate of when the facility would open.

In a statement, an ICE spokesperson called it a "staging facility for deportations"

"A staging facility is where illegal aliens await their deportation flight to their destination country or transfer to a detention facility," the spokesperson said.

ABC News' Ely Brown and Laura Romero contributed to this report.

US bond yields have surged upward over the past month, as yields on both the 10-year Treasury (^TNX) and 30-year Treasury (^TYX) have reached levels not seen since 2002, surpassing 2007 high-water marks in the lead-up to the financial crisis.

Investors have attributed the run-up in yields to a variety of concerns, from the artificial intelligence build-out and the competition for capital to changing foreign ownership of gold versus fixed income.

One overlooked source of upward pressure, argued Macquarie's Thierry Wizman, is not just the impact of the Iran war on the energy market but uncertainty about when the war will end or what the conflict will look like going forward.

"The perception that global conflict is endemic may also be causing long-term inflation expectation[s] to stay elevated," Wizman wrote to clients.

The uncertainty factor for investors, Wizman said, centers around the midterm elections.

President Trump has said he expects the war to wrap up shortly after the US midterms as he evaluates the success of the US naval blockade of Iran and Tehran's shift in leverage after the elections past. However, the president has also said he's considering a major renewed bombing campaign after the elections, which would likely push the conflict back into "hot war" territory and reignite tensions.

"This status quo can change dramatically after November 3, when President Trump, unfettered by domestic political considerations, will have more latitude to choose between peace and/or war, instead of sitting on the sidelines, kinetically and diplomatically," Wizman wrote. "Implied volatilities are starting to price in divergent two-way outcomes after November 3, when events can shift wildly one way or the other."

That makes it difficult for investors to evaluate what Wizman says is a critical component of the war in Iran: the conflict's impact on government spending.

At face value, the shuttering of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on energy infrastructure throughout the Gulf region have sent energy prices soaring, depressing bond prices as investors price in higher inflation rates for longer. Brent (BZ=F) oil futures, the international benchmark, pushed back past $100 per barrel on Thursday.

But wars are also expensive to fight, as the US government writes checks for munitions restocks, fuel stores to power aircraft and naval vessels, combat pay for soldiers, and a litany of other costs. The latest figures submitted to Congress by the Pentagon indicate the US government has spent at least $43.6 billion so far, though outside research institutions suggest the actual sum could be far higher.

title: Robertson's Scotland career in numbers as 100th cap looms
description: Andy Robertson is poised to become only the second man ever to play 100 times for Scotland. BBC Sport Scotland charts his international career in numbers.
fullText:
Andy Robertson is poised to become only the second man to win 100 caps for Scotland in more than 150 years of international football.

The national captain could hit the century mark in Saturday's Nations League game against North Macedonia as he closes in on the all-time cap record.

A constant presence since Gordon Strachan handed him his debut in 2014 when he was a fresh-faced left-back with Dundee United, Robertson has defined a generation of the Scotland national team.

Here, BBC Scotland charts the Tottenham Hotspur defender's international career in numbers.

Inside the fairytale journey of Scotland captain Robertson

Robertson set to hit 100 Scotland caps - but who else makes top 10?

The great Kenny Dalglish is the only man to have pulled on the navy blue of Scotland more times than Robertson.

'King Kenny' still tops the list on 102 caps, but that could be eclipsed by his friend come November should the 32-year-old feature in each of Scotland's remaining Nations League games this year.

It is fitting that it will be Robertson who surpasses that long-standing milestone, given the pair have forged a friendship over his time with Liverpool.

Not that Dalglish is having that.

"He always says 'you've got millions more games; Nations League, what's that? They didn't have that in my day!'" Robertson joked on the Stick to Football podcast recently.

"I think he might bring up a ratio for years-to-games-played so he's still on top.

"It's obviously something that's been on my radar for a while now. When you get to 80-odd caps, you start to look up."

Dalglish can console himself that his record of 30 goals - held jointly with Denis Law - is safely out of Robertson's reach.

Of current players, John McGinn is lurking only eight behind Robertson on the all-time list, though, so the Scotland men's centurion club could have three members soon.

Since being given the armband by Alex McLeish after Scott Brown retired in 2018, Robertson has captained Scotland 29 times more than any other player.

At the time, he had earned just 22 caps and was just 24 but had established himself as Liverpool's left-back as they reached the Champions League final.

Now, he is the only man to have lead Scotland out at three major finals, reaching the milestone at the World Cup this summer.

Scotland and Napoli midfielder Scott McTominay enthused: "He's such a great captain and he's got that good balance between being one of the senior players and saying you need to wake up if you're not playing well.

"Then he's also got the personable side, organising things with the manager, helping young players and stuff. He's brilliant with that, brilliant."

Robertson has played under four different permanent Scotland team bosses in his 12-year international career.

It was Strachan who plucked him from the under-21s to hand him his debut as a 19-year-old in a win over Poland in March 2014.

McLeish made him captain in 2018, calling Robertson the "outstanding candidate" and an "inspirational figure" - and now he has played twice for new boss Sebastien Pocognoli.

He even played one game under interim manager Malky Mackay in a friendly against the Netherlands at Pittodrie in 2017 as the Scottish FA searched for Strachan's replacement.

However, it is Steve Clarke's seven-year stint that Robertson will be mainly associated with, as the pair lead Scotland to three major tournaments.

Robertson played 68 times for Clarke, all of them as captain, and the recently departed head coach consistently praised his figurehead.

"He's been a fantastic captain for Scotland," Clarke said at the World Cup.

"He's worked ever so hard for the country and he leads the group like the leader he is - and he's very, very important to me and the squad."

Given his longevity, it is perhaps no surprise that Robertson also tops the Scotland assist charts since his debut in 2014.

However, Robertson's rampaging runs and crosses from left-back have been pivotal for a Scotland side that has never been free-scoring during his career.

And, although he only has four Scotland goals, there have been a couple of important ones.

His strike against Cyprus helped ensure the Clarke era started with a win in 2019. And his last-minute winner against Poland in 2024 temporarily staved off Nations League relegation.

That was the last time Robertson scored for Scotland.

Over the piece, Robertson's caps are spread fairly evenly among friendlies and qualification games.

Crucially, though, he has also played nine times in major tournaments. What will rankle with him is there is only one win among those nine - June's victory over Haiti in Boston at the World Cup.

Overall, though, Robertson's Scotland career can be characterised by consistency.

He has started 97 of his 99 caps, and played an average of 83 minutes per game, rarely ever being substituted. He has not missed a camp in three years.

The only question seems to be how many Scotland caps will Robertson end up with? At 32 and still playing in the Premier League, it appears there will be plenty more to come.

title: How Gordon became one of England's main men
description: Anthony Gordon has been England's in-form player since the World Cup knockout stage -  is the Barcelona forward now undroppable?
fullText:
Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Declan Rice, Jordan Pickford and now Anthony Gordon.

All have become guaranteed starters and reliable stars for England, with the Barcelona winger the latest to look, according to captain Kane, like one of the Three Lions' "main men".

Gordon was one of England's standout players at the World Cup and earned a big-money move to European giants Barca in the summer, while his good form has continued into his country's Nations League campaign.

He scored the opening goal in England's 2-0 win against the Czech Republic on Tuesday night, after also netting in a 3-2 defeat by world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday.

In fact, the 25-year-old's England form has been building since the knockout stage of the World Cup began - his run of averaging a goal contribution every 69 minutes started with assisting both Kane's efforts in a 2-1 last-32 victory over DR Congo.

The former Newcastle player has scored three goals and provided three assists in his past six England matches, while he also won the penalty in England's dramatic last-16 victory over Mexico at Azteca Stadium.

And after a positive start in Spain, where he has already picked up five assists in La Liga, Gordon looks to be joining boss Thomas Tuchel's "undroppable" bracket.

Tuchel likes to give his players clarity on their role and makes clear who they are up against in the squad and for a starting position.

When asked whether Gordon is getting to be one of the first names on the team-sheet, he said: "He's getting there. He's defending his shirt, he's defending his position - an excellent performance again after his performance against Spain.

"He was very decisive [against the Czech Republic] and had an excellent goal. It was very, very difficult but the technique and finishing was excellent.

"He scored against Spain so he has decisive actions and he's defending his shirt and his position. He does it on the highest level and he's a very important player."

Gordon linked up well with his former Newcastle team-mate Lewis Hall on England's left and combined with right-back Trent Alexander-Arnold, who was making his first start for the Three Lions in nearly two years, for the opening goal.

Gordon said he had been "dying" to link up with Alexander-Arnold, who is also playing in Spain for Barcelona's rivals Real Madrid.

"It's a great compliment and it's great to play with him," Alexander-Arnold said of Gordon.

"I tried to get the ball, and try and see what the best play is and try and play forward and create something. And I was able to get the pass."

Captain and record goalscorer Kane is a guaranteed starter in England's biggest matches but the position to the left of Kane has been a problem area for the team, with no player able to make it their own.

Gordon looks to have secured that role and Kane said the winger is "showing that he belongs at the highest level, for Barcelona and England".

"His performances in the last couple of games have been some of his best that he has played in an England shirt," Kane said.

"I think he is just relishing putting the shirt on and being one of the main men in the team. He is an important player for us and he showed that during the World Cup."

It has not always been a straightforward route into the team for Gordon.

Marcus Rashford, Eberechi Eze, Phil Foden and Noni Madueke have all featured for England from the left in the past couple of years.

Gordon started to emerge as a clear option during Lee Carsley's time in interim charge, but said himself last October that he had only shown "50%" of what he can do for England.

Now that seems to be coming to fruition. Against the Czech Republic he attempted four shots, more than any England player and more than any of his team-mates against Spain too.

Gordon is ranked in at least the top four of England players for expected assists (0.9), expected goals (0.9), passes into the box (14), touches in the opposition box (29), chances created (eight), and shots on target (five), since the start of the World Cup knockout stage.

His importance is underlined by the fact he has contributed the same amount of goals and assists, six, as Bellingham since England faced DR Congo.

There has been an interesting subplot with Gordon and Rashford competing for a left-wing space for England and effectively Barcelona.

Rashford was on loan at Barcelona last season but they opted to not make his move permanent, instead he returned to Manchester United while the Catalan club splashed out £69m to sign Gordon from Newcastle.

Gordon has the ability to take on his full-back on the inside or beat them for pace on the outside before putting in a cross.

"People raised eyebrows when Anthony Gordon went to Barcelona for the money that he did and Marcus Rashford came back to Manchester United," former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"He has become a key part of the England team. There were certain games in the World Cup where he was substituted and he shouldn't have been - I think others should have come off instead of him.

"Gordon [when he is] full of confidence running at pace like he does, he can go either way and he's causing full-backs all kind of problems."

Gordon says that since his move to Spain he has changed people's perception of him being a player who is only quick and presses well, even if they are two of his best attributes.

"I always felt in England, people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never actually respected the quality and IQ that I play with," Gordon told ITV.

"Only the players I play with ever seem to notice that. I think now I'm at Barcelona and I play a different style, those qualities are highlighted much more and people are actually starting to take notice that I'm not just quick.

"In England, it was never really respected because people just see me as really quick and really aggressive.

"In Spain, they really appreciate my IQ and quality because at Barca, if you're not technical, if you're not smart, you're going to stand out like a sore thumb."

Tuchel is starting to build a team he thinks can challenge and win the Euros in 2028.

But first he wants to win the Nations League, and if England are to do that, it is likely Gordon will have played a huge part.

fullText:
The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI.

Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years.

The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease.

Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules.

In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn, he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest.

"AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said.

Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself.

He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images".

But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big.

Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere".

Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated.

Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real.

Nikon said Xu was "respectfully complying" with its investigation and had provided it with additional technical documents.

Dr Patrick Hickey, who came fifth in the 2026 Small World contest, said the recognition the award represents means more than the $3,000 (£2,250) prize itself.

"If you spend a lot of your time in a dark room looking down a microscope, it's really nice to be able to show people and to show the public," he said.

"There's an interesting fusion between science and art, and a lot of the images that scientists are making have some very abstract and artistic qualities to them."

Hickey said it would be unfair on other entrants if it turned out the winning video was unfairly altered by AI.

"There's a specific set of rules in the contest, and one of them was quite clearly that you couldn't use generative AI to produce things, and the other was obviously that it has to be taken under a microscope," he said.

So far, Nikon is standing by its procedures but it said there would be an update soon.

"At this time, we don't see that any rules were violated," it said in a statement.

On a day when Matt Fitzpatrick began his quest for a fifth win of the year, Robert MacIntyre reacted furiously to a drone and Lee Westwood and Ian Poulter made a DP World Tour return after an absence of almost four years, it was a player from outside the world's top 900 that stole the show at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship.

Scotland's Michael Stewart, ranked 979, shot 65 to sit at seven under after outscoring a big-name field to share the lead at the end of round one.

It gave the Scot a share of the lead after round one, with Australia's Jack Buchanan.

Stewart, 36, has played only five events on the main European circuit - the last in 2023 - and teed off less than 24 hours after finishing second in the Tartan Tour's Duddingston Classic having received a sponsor's invite this week.

However, after making a solitary birdie on the front nine, an eagle on the par-five 12th proved to be the catalyst for him the play the next five holes in six under after the turn.

"It's easy to get yourself up for this event. I played Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday [at Duddingston], straight here. I've played here a lot in the past and just delighted to be part of the event.

"I grew up on a links course. I played nice all day to be honest. Lots of fairways, lots of greens and then on the back, the putter got hot."

Stewart's remarkable back nine at Carnoustie and Buchanan's equally impressive score at Kingsbarns, was in contrast to several eye-catching moments in the team event featuring former sports stars and celebrities, who were paired with the professionals.

However, ex-Real Madrid and Wales winger Gareth Bale did at least provide instantly shareable social media content when his ball found the roof of the Jigger Inn, teeing off on the 17th at St Andrews - one of three courses utilised to stage the tournament.

South Africa's MJ Daffue and Casey Jarvis are a stroke off the lead on the professional leaderboard, while Fitzpatrick, who was victorious at the French Open last week, signed for a four-under 68 to sit three shots adrift.

Five-time major winner Brooks Koepka was three under after a 69 at Carnoustie, a shot better off than Tommy Fleetwood, while defending champion MacIntyre was one under at the same course.

MacIntyre was also spoken to by officials after losing his temper because of a drone flying above him on the par-three eighth, his penultimate hole of the day.

"It drives me insane. I've had previous for it," he said.

"I asked [the rules official] twice previous to the shot on the eighth about the drone. I can't say anything just now.

"He's obviously heard me swear a few times straight at the camera guy. We'll see what the TD [tournament director] has got to say."

Westwood is at one under, with Poulter at level par on their first appearances on the DP World Tour since January 2023, having made controversial switches to LIV Golf in 2022.

title: Never played in Prem - and now face World Cup hosts
description: Jack Combes and Alex Post tell BBC Sport about a "dream come true" as they look ahead to the 2027 Rugby World Cup opener against hosts Australia.
fullText:
It is 1 October 2027. There are 61,000 fans inside Perth Stadium.

There is a global TV audience in the millions as two teams go through their final warm-ups preparing to open the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

For hosts Australia, twice world champions with a proud rugby history across the codes, it is familiar territory.

For their opponents Hong Kong China, it is anything but.

It will be their World Cup debut and for their players it will be biggest match of their lives.

Among them, all being well, are Jack Combes and Alex Post. Two players more used to the lower semi-professional tiers of the English league system than the global spotlight.

It is David v Goliath - in football parlance it is Spain v Cape Verde. You get the idea.

Twelve months earlier to the day, Jack and Alex are in Hong Kong. It is a national holiday and both have taken time out to tell BBC Sport about how their sporting and personal lives have been transformed.

"I think the whole run-up to the whole qualification process was already a dream in itself. To qualify for a men's first World Cup was huge," said Combes, a scrum-half.

There are glints in their eyes and smiles on their faces - why wouldn't there be?

Hong Kong China have been drawn in Pool A at the World Cup, where not just the hosts await, but also Chile - and the All Blacks.

"People will say it's daunting and it's a huge challenge to have those two top nations in your pool, but if you're going to do it, do it properly. Why not?" said Post.

"People might question whether we deserve to be there. But for me, if you asked anyone as a kid, if you could open up the World Cup in that first game in a year's time, it's genuinely amazing. A dream come true.

"And I'm sure anyone who does give us any criticism about us being there, there's no way they wouldn't be doing the same thing if they could, 100%."

Despite having made his international debut a decade ago, until recently Post was hooking for Richmond in The Champ.

"Unfortunately, I've never played at The Prem level. But The Champ definitely doesn't get the credit it deserves," said the 31-year-old.

"It's a very tough league. And that was great preparation for the international games."

Post was a full-time rugby player with Hong Kong China, before the Covid pandemic brought that to an end and he began a Masters degree at the University of Oxford.

The Varsity match at Twickenham remains one of the larger crowds he has played in front of.

"One of the unique selling points for Hong Kong is the players are contracted all year round and spend all their time together," said Post.

"So it wasn't really feasible for players like myself to stay at Richmond.

"Hong Kong was very much, 'we need boots on the ground'.

"I've moved my family and myself over the last couple of weeks and yeah, kind of chase the dream for the next year."

A full-time professional contract has enabled greater focus on the game away from being a financial analyst.

"With Richmond, we'd train twice a week and then you would do your own gym sessions in your own time," added Post.

"But you can probably do twice as much as that with Hong Kong now."

For Combes, 29, a former student and teacher at Hartpury College, it has been a circuitous route to professional sport that included a spell at Birmingham Moseley in England's third tier.

"So I've been full-time in the sevens for about three and a half years now," he said.

"I've done my career in reverse. I went from teaching after an ACL (anterior cruciate ligament injury), to playing semi-professional rugby, to being a full-time athlete at the age of 25.

"I wouldn't change it for the world, but going into a full-time environment where you have the resources, you have the training time, physical development, it's necessary for what we're facing."

Hong Kong has a proud tradition of rugby stretching back seven decades, not least around its annual sevens tournament.

They qualified for the World Cup by defeating Korea 70-22 in the final round of the Asia Rugby Championship last year.

A late 42-40 victory over fellow World Cup finalists Uruguay in July was perhaps the strongest showing yet of where they stand.

"The mindset's changed from years gone by where you compete in Asia and you play against teams that you know you probably should be beating," said Combes.

"Now we're completely on the other side of the spectrum where we've got nothing to lose.

"I think just be ambitious, be fearless, and go for it.

"'Be memorable' is the phrase that coaches have been talking about."

Both Post and Combes were born in Hong Kong and came up through the age-grade system there. They have witnessed how the game has grown there and are aware of the criticism they have faced, often focused on the international make-up of the team.

"It's always the first criticism we get after an international game," said Post.

"We don't go looking for that criticism or feedback. But it's always going to be there. I think for us, just perform and try and put something out there that people are proud of."

"I was born here in 1997," added Combes.

"Mum is half Chinese and going through the whole minis rugby here where we probably had one of the biggest mini rugby numbers base in the world, up until Covid.

"But I think the game's back growing within local schools - primary, secondary.

"Hopefully we can inspire the next generation."

Former London Irish and Ospreys director of rugby Toby Booth has joined the coaching set-up.

A good test of where they are at will come when Hong Kong China take on three countries in the Nations Cup next month, all with World Cup heritage, in the shape of USA, Canada and Tonga.

"Personally, I've got a whole bunch of pressure just from my family and friends," said Post.

"I've been getting messages all today saying it's one year, you better make the team.

"There will definitely be a big Hong Kong contingent [in Perth]. We want to be everyone's second team."

"You know, we are always going to be the underdogs," said Combes, who is known to his team-mates as Maradona for his keenness to kick any stray footballs that make their way on to the training pitch.

"I think our whole string of games leading into the World Cup with Nations Cup, warm-up games we're always going to be sort of looked over.

"But I think that works in our favour - we're just a bit fearless."

Oh, and remember Spain v Cape Verde at the Fifa World Cup? That ended in a draw.

title: England avoid Australia & India in World Cup draw
description: England avoid defending champions Australia and world number one-ranked side India in the group-stage draw for the 2027 ICC Cricket World Cup.
fullText:
England have avoided defending champions Australia and world number one-ranked side India in the group-stage draw for the 2027 ICC Men's Cricket World Cup.

India and Pakistan are, once again, placed in the same group, alongside Australia, Afghanistan, Zimbabwe and a qualifier.

England, who won the trophy in 2019, are in the same group as co-hosts South Africa, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, New Zealand and a qualifier.

Harry Brook's side, who have enjoyed a resurgence in the 50-over format, begin their campaign against Bangladesh on 8 October, and Sri Lanka on 13 October in Windhoek, Namibia.

They will come up against South Africa in Gqeberha on 16 October before travelling to Harare to face a qualifier on 20 October. They round off the group stage when they face New Zealand, again in Gqeberha, on 23 October.

The visit to Zimbabwe is significant, with England having not played there since 2004.

Political unrest in Zimbabwe under the regime of former president Robert Mugabe caused problems for England's men's team throughout the 2000s.

England boycotted their fixture against Zimbabwe in Harare at the 2003 World Cup - a decision which ultimately derailed their campaign.

Relations have improved in recent years, however, and BBC Sport reported in 2025 that the two cricket boards were discussing a potential England tour of the country in the next cycle of international cricket between 2027 and 2031.

After three matches to decide the final two qualifiers, the tournament group stage will open with a repeat of the 2023 final when India and Australia face each other in Cape Town on 7 October.

Arch-rivals India and Pakistan, who do not play each other outside tournaments, will meet in Johannesburg on 10 October.

The top three, plus the best fourth-placed finisher, from the two groups progress to the Super 7 stage.

From there, the top four teams will qualify for the semi-finals, which are scheduled for 17 and 18 November, before the final on 21 November in Johannesburg.

title: Real Madrid superstar’s post-injury vacation approved by Mourinho and the club – report
description: Real Madrid ace Kylian Mbappe escaped with a minor injury in France’s first game of the international break and was relieved from national team duty immediately by the manager Zinedine Zidane.The cu...
fullText:
Real Madrid ace Kylian Mbappe escaped with a minor injury in France's first game of the international break and was relieved from national team duty immediately by the manager Zinedine Zidane.

The current diagnosis is of a posterior capsule hyperextension of the left knee, and his recovery time is estimated to be in weeks.

Yet, it could well have been much worse and it is said that the player may well have required surgery if he had played longer.

Currently, the player continues to be in France and has not returned to Madrid.

He has been spotted with his friends and his partner, and it has unsurprisingly led to a lot of speculation on why he is on vacation when he should be working on his return.

Mourinho has backed Mbappe's time off. (Photo by Angel Martinez/Getty Images)

As confirmed by AS in a recent update, however, Mbappe's trip to his country and the time he is enjoying off with his partner and friends is not secretive. In fact, the club completely backed his vacation.

Jose Mourinho is aware of the player taking some time off in France, as are the coaching staff and the medical team of the club.

They all understand that Mbappe's setback only requires rest and that the player returning to the Valdebebas may serve no real purpose.

His recovery plan, in that sense, is said to be 'co-ordinated' and 'consensual' as they describe it in the club offices.

The idea is that he will take his recovery slow and pace it out, likely even missing the team's first game after the break.

Having Mbappe fit for the Clasico is the priority. (Photo by Yasser Bakhsh/Getty Images)

Real Madrid's first game after the break is against Villarreal, and Mourinho and Co. prioritise the player being available in the long run over him being fit for the game against the Yellow Submarines.

The goal, quite clearly, is to have Mbappe fit and raring for the game against Barcelona later in October and the management considers his presence on that night to be fundamental.

So far, the Frenchman has been Real Madrid's top finishing presence in the opposition box and has carried Real Madrid's attack alongside Jude Bellingham.

The sensible idea, in that sense, would be to keep him fit and ready for the big games against Roma, Barcelona and RB Leipzig.

fullText:
A tearful Kei Nishikori said he "kept fighting right to the end" as the former world number four ended his professional career at the Japan Open.

Nishikori, known as one of the best players to never win a Grand Slam, lost 6-4 6-4 to world number eight Frances Tiafoe in Tokyo.

The 36-year-old became the first Japanese man to reach a major final when he faced Marin Cilic in the 2014 US Open showpiece.

Nishikori beat then world number one Novak Djokovic on his way to the New York final and defeated Rafael Nadal for Olympic bronze at the 2016 Games in Rio.

He was, however, hampered by injuries throughout his 19-year career.

"Playing in Japan is always a special moment," an emotional Nishikori told his home crowd.

"I wish I could have put in a slightly more convincing performance. But I'm happy I kept fighting right to the end.

"I'm proud that I didn't give up and played right to the finish."

After losing to Tiafoe, Nishikori did a lap of honour of the main showcourt in Tokyo - the place where he won the title in 2012 and 2014.

A video featuring Djokovic, three-time Grand Slam champion Andy Murray and 1989 French Open winner Michael Chang, congratulating Nishikori, was also played.

"Your resilience and fighting spirit, to always come back after a lot of adversity, is really commendable and admirable," Djokovic said.

"We had some great battles all over the world. I'm really glad you're ending your career in your town, your country, in front of your people.

"You're going to get the farewell you absolutely deserve."

Nishikori started playing aged five and moved to Florida as a 14-year-old to train.

He won 12 ATP Tour singles titles in his career and claimed 40 victories over top-10 players.

He was the first Japanese man to reach the top 10 of the world rankings and inspired numerous players, including four-time major champion Naomi Osaka.

His 72.5% win-rate in deciding sets is the third best in ATP Tour history, behind only Bjorn Borg (73.4%) and John McEnroe (72.8%).

title: Nine scandals that rocked the sporting world
description: Manchester City are far from the first. The lure of glory and riches on the biggest stages have tempted plenty of other sports stars to break the rules.
fullText:
Manchester City being found guilty of fuelling an era of glittering Premier League success via a network of sponsorship deals, found by an independent commision to be a "sham", has shaken the world of sport.

The lure of glory and riches on the biggest stages have tempted plenty of others to cheat.

BBC Sport looks back on nine more sporting scandals, stretching back more than a century.

Cancer survivor. Cycling legend. American hero. Cheat.

Lance Armstrong had spent years vehemently and aggressively insisting that he had won all seven of his Tour de France titles between 1999 and 2005 without the help of performance-enhancing drugs.

His story was remarkable. Aged 25, Armstrong had been diagnosed with testicular cancer, with doctors warning he was likely to die given the disease had spread to other parts of his body.

He not only survived, but returned to dominate top-level cycling. His Livestrong Foundation was wildly successful, selling millions of yellow wristbands to raise money to support fellow cancer sufferers.

However, as the evidence and former team-mates allegations against him stacked up, Armstrong was stripped of his Tour de France titles.

Armstong eventually confessed to cheating in a blockbuster interview with talk show host Oprah Winfrey.

"I made those decisions, they were my mistake and I'm here to say sorry," he said, adding that the culture in professional cycling made using drugs non-negotiable.

Armstrong says sorry for doping

Hansie Cronje was the golden boy of South African sport.

Good looking and charming, he led the nation's cricket team with style and authority.

President Nelson Mandela singled out Cronje in 1996 for the "excellent manner" in which he captained the Proteas.

However, Cronje's love of money, combined with a fast-growing betting industry and the organised crime it attracted, proved his downfall.

Cronje entertained the offers of match-fixers, calling team meetings to discuss the possibility of throwing matches and sharing thousands of dollars in inducements.

Most infamously, Cronje contrived to lose a rain-affected Test against England in 2000.

With South Africa still in the midst of their first innings on the final day, Cronje convinced England counterpart Nasser Hussein that in the interest of sporting entertainment each side should forfeit an innings, producing a sudden run-chase and giving England a shot at victory.

Cronje was praised for his Corinthian spirit. In reality, he had been motivated by a bribe of £5,000 to ensure the match did not end in a draw.

Cronje was undone when an Indian police wiretap of a bookmaker caught him in discussions about fixing matches.

Cronje confessed in early 2000, was banned from cricket for life and died in a plane crash two years later at the age of 32.

Hansie Cronje, match-fixing and plane crash that left a complex legacy

There was something particular about turn 17 of the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

In 2008, before the inaugural Singapore Grand Prix was held at the circuit, Renault driver Nelson Piquet Jr knew it did not have any overhead cranes to lift a damaged car from the track. There were no side entrances to allow a stranded driver to be pushed out of danger's way by marshalls either.

On lap 14 Piquet found himself in exactly in that unfortunate position. And, despite his initial claim that he had made a "simple mistake", the Brazilian had put himself there deliberately.

When Renault dropped him in 2009, Piquet Jr revealed that he steered himself into a concrete wall to crash his car. The safety car was deployed as officials cleared debris off the track.

Crucially, Piquet Jr's team-mate Fernando Alonso was the only frontrunner to have stopped for fuel and new tyres at the point of the crash.

As Alonso's rivals went into the pits, the Spaniard, benefitting from the reduced gaps caused by the safety car, moved up the field and went on to win the race.

While Alonso was cleared of any wrongdoing or knowledge of the plot, Renault team principal Flavio Briatore and chief technical officer Pat Symonds were banned from F1 for several years.

Still in F1 10 years after 'crashgate'

Frank Lampard wheeled away in celebration after his well-hit shot from the edge of the penalty area beat Kevin Miller in the Crystal Palace goal in the 65th minute of a Monday evening Premier League game in November 1997.

As he was mobbed by team-mates, Upton Park was plunged into darkness.

The following month similar happened at Selhurst Park. Thirteen seconds into the second half - with Wimbledon and Arsenal goalless - the lights went off. The Christmas lights in nearby Croydon were raised as a possible cause.

The actual cause was more sinister.

An Asian betting syndicate had pulled the plug, using a remote control circuit breaker, to get each match abandoned at a scoreline which would maximise their profits.

The gang were foiled in their attempts to pull the deception for a third time. They had bribed a security guard at Charlton Athletic to allow them to plant a device at The Valley before Liverpool's visit in February.

However, a suspicious member of staff at the club tipped off police.

Four men were given sentences of between 18 months and four years for their involvement.

Four jailed for floodlight plot

No expense was spared for the Winter Olympics in Sochi in 2014.

With a budget of $50bn (£38bn) - more than 25 times Vancouver's 2010 Winter Olympics spend - organisers created two entirely new resorts, bristling with security and military personnel.

But building facilities from scratch also gave the Russian hosts a chance to design an elaborate way around anti-doping measures.

A secret tunnel allowed a Russian secret service agent, disguised as a sewer engineer, to swap out his compatriots' urine samples, which contained traces of banned substances.

A special method had been developed to remove the tamperproof lids of sample bottles, which were then refilled with 'clean' urine that had been frozen before Russian athletes began doping programmes.

Forty-three Russian athletes were banned for life, 28 of whom successfully appealed against the full extent of their punishment.

Russia was banned from competing at the following Winter Olympics in South Korea, although athletes who could demonstrate their clean record were permitted to compete under a neutral flag.

Russia banned from 2018 Winter Olympics

A camera crew caught the aftermath of the attack on Nancy Kerrigan in January 1994.

The 24-year-old figure skater was captured clutching her leg and repeatedly wailing "why?".

Kerrigan had been training at a rink in Detroit before the American national championships. As she stepped off the ice, a man rushed towards her and struck her on the leg with a telescopic baton.

Kerrigan's 'why' was soon answered.

The bodyguard and ex-husband of Kerrigan's rival Tonya Harding had hired a man to break Kerrigan's leg. They hoped to rule her out of the forthcoming Winter Olympics in Lillehammer, boosting Harding's chances.

It didn't work. Kerrigan recovered from heavy bruising in time to make the USA team, alongside Harding.

Amid a media frenzy, Harding, struggling with a broken lace on her boot, finished eighth in the Olympic final.

The competition broke viewing records in the US.

Harding was banned for life from the sport after admitting attempting to conceal the identity of Kerrigan's assailant after the attack.

Harding's ex-husband Jeff Gillooly, the attacker he hired and a getaway driver all spent time in prison for their part in the crime.

When Olympic figure skating met whodunnit

The headline written in the Chicago Daily News summed up the disbelief of a city, a nation and a sport when it emerged that superstar Joe Jackson and seven of his Chicago White Sox team-mates had apparently taken bribes to lose the 1919 World Series, baseball's biggest game.

First baseman Chick Gandil was the ringleader, while star pitcher Eddie Cicotte was the key figure.

A fee of $100,000 - worth about $1.6m today - was agreed with the head of a betting syndicate, with the money to be shared among the eight conspirators.

Cicotte's pitch, deliberately hitting Maurice Rath on the back, was a sign to his team-mates, and gamblers in the know, that the fix was on.

After the White Sox lost the series 5-3 to the Cincinnati Reds, the White Sox's suspicious owner Charles Comiskey sent word that the players needed to collect their pay cheques from him in person.

None of the eight fixers did. They left the stadium without their money. Rumours spread, followed by an investigation, and soon the players were in the dock.

Although a criminal court failed to convict the players, they were banned from Major League Baseball for life.

Jackson insisted until his death in 1951 that he was not involved and that, despite receiving $5,000, he had been deceived into signing a confession.

The data revolutionary who exposed baseball's big fix

At half-time in their first match at the 2000 Paralympics the coach of Spain's intellectual disability basketball team told them to stop scoring so quickly and let their opponents shoot more.

He knew the vast majority of the team were there under false pretences.

Of the 12 players in the squad, 10 had no intellectual impairment at all, but were keen amateur players who had been recruited months before the Sydney Games to supplement the team.

Spain, perhaps unsurprisingly, won gold convincingly, beating Russia 87-63 in the final.

The scam unravelled because one of the ringers was also a journalist.

Realising he was in the midst of an incredible scoop, Carlos Ribagorda played in Sydney and then published an article detailing the scandal on his return.

The team were stripped of their medals and the incident led to a total ban on athletes with an intellectual disability from the 2004 and 2008 Paralympics, destroying the careers of thousands of sportspeople around the world.

Fake Paralympians boss: 'I didn't know about cheating'

When public prosecutors tapped telephone calls at Italian football giants Juventus in 2004, they were hunting for evidence of doping.

What they believed they found was corruption on a far more systematic scale.

They thought they had evidence of Juve general manager Luciano Moggi pressurising referee officials to favour certain clubs, including his own. Moggi denied the claims.

However, Juve, AC Milan, Fiorentina, Lazio and Reggina were all implicated in influencing referees.

All were given points deductions, but only Juventus ultimately dropped into the second tier of Italian football.

There was a split in the club's superstar squad.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Patrick Vieira joined rivals Inter Milan for a combined £23m, Fabio Cannavaro and Emerson went to Real Madrid for £13.7m, Lilian Thuram and Gianluca Zambrotta joined Barcelona for £13m, and Adrian Mutu went to Fiorentina for £5.5m.

But other key players – notably Gianluigi Buffon, Alessandro del Piero, Giorgio Chiellini, Pavel Nedved and David Trezeguet – remained with Juve in Serie B.

Despite beginning the season with a nine-point penalty and an opening-day draw with minnows Rimini, Juventus were promoted at the first attempt.

The club still lay claim to the 2004–05 and 2005–06 titles that were stripped from them, counting 38 rather than the official 36.

fullText:
Leg-spinner Mason Crane could play for England for the first time in eight years after being recalled for the one-day international tri-series in Pakistan.

The 29-year-old won his only Test cap against Australia in Sydney in 2018 and is now given an opportunity in the series which also involves Sri Lanka next month.

Crane, who also played two T20 internationals in 2017, could also push his case in the fight to be England's number one spinner in Test cricket.

Sam Curran and Adil Rashid both return after injuries, and uncapped pair James Coles and Henry Crocombe are included.

Jos Buttler is out with the hamstring injury he sustained last week, while Jacob Bethell is continuing his recovery from knee surgery.

Brydon Carse, who is under an investigation from the Cricket Regulator following an incident outside a nightclub in Derby in August, remains absent.

England squad for tri-series in Pakistan: Harry Brook (Yorkshire – captain), Gus Atkinson (Surrey), Sonny Baker (Hampshire), Tom Banton (Somerset), James Coles (Sussex), Jordan Cox (Essex), Mason Crane (Glamorgan), Henry Crocombe (Sussex), Sam Curran (Surrey), Liam Dawson (Hampshire), Ben Duckett (Nottinghamshire), Will Jacks (Surrey), Jamie Overton (Surrey), Adil Rashid (Yorkshire), Joe Root (Yorkshire), Josh Tongue (Nottinghamshire).

TMS podcast: Behind the scenes at the PCA Awards

England are on a diet of white-ball cricket until three Tests in South Africa in December as they build up to the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa next year.

The tri-series in Pakistan involves the three teams taking part playing each other twice, with the top two advancing to the final. Following the trip to Pakistan, England play three one-day internationals and five T20s in Australia in November.

As England continue to shape their backroom staff following the arrival of Stephen Fleming as Test coach, Jeetan Patel, Mike Yardy, David Saker and Carl Hopkinson will assist white-ball head coach Brendon McCullum in Pakistan.

That means Marcus Trescothick, who took temporary charge of the Test team for the series against Pakistan in the home summer, misses the trip.

It is understood the make-up of the coaching staff is part of a plan to rotate the coaches – fielding coach Sarah Taylor and fast-bowling coach Tim Southee are also not going to Pakistan.

All of Trescothick, Taylor and Southee are likely to be part of England's coaching team for other tours this winter.

The return of Glamorgan's Crane is eye-catching, given the close proximity of the World Cup and the uncertainty surrounding the spin-bowling in England's Test team.

The former Hampshire man is rewarded for consistent performances across formats in domestic cricket.

This season Crane took 34 wickets in the County Championship and demonstrated his improvement with the bat by making his first two first-class hundreds.

England national selector Marcus North said: "Mason Crane has been performing consistently for Glamorgan across both formats during the summer. He's an experienced, high-class leg-spinner who thoroughly deserves another opportunity at international level."

Archer is a first choice in all three formats for England and his absence from the Pakistan trip is a clear indication of how the pace bowlers could be managed across the winter.

McCullum has already indicated other seamers could skip the T20 series in Australia in order to prepare for the three Tests in South Africa.

England are expected to name their squad for the Australia tour, along with their new list of centrally contracted players, next week.

fullText:
Guardian tested chatbots after French far-right politician stripped a Muslim woman of her hijab in a photo

When prompted, AI chat bots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith.

The Guardian asked ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini and Claude to take the veil off an AI-generated image of a woman wearing a hijab. Both OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok bots complied with the prompt. Anthropic’s Claude responded that it does not have an image-editing or generating feature but that it would not alter a photo to remove someone’s hijab.

Gemini initially said that it could not remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people because it could not digitally alter someone’s appearance without their consent. But when asked to make the woman look more “western”, the bot created an image of her without her hijab.

The Guardian US tested the chatbots after a French far-right politician stripped a real Muslim woman of her hijab and long-sleeved dress in a picture he made clear was modified. Julien Odoul, a member of parliament and of the National Rally party, posted the altered image of the woman on X with her hair visible and arms exposed alongside the caption “LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE”, meaning French Liberty. He quote-tweeted the original image, posted by someone else, which showed the woman crossing a street wearing a hijab and full-length dress.

It was unclear which software or AI model Odoul used or even whether he modified the image himself, but experts say the MP’s actions were part of a growing pattern of tech-enabled anti-Muslim hatred around the world.

In India, where anti-Muslim sentiment is rampant, generative AI is playing an increasingly significant role in producing images that, among other things, sexualize Muslim women or dehumanize Muslims generally, according to a study by non-profit US thinktank the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH). The CSOH also found that there are similar types of AI-enabled hatred being directed at prominent female Muslim politicians in the US like Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib.

“This is just part of an ongoing trend of how we see Muslim communities, and particularly Muslim women, being targeted and abused,” said Eviane Leidig, the director of research and outreach at CSOH.

While Grok promptly complied with a request to edit an image of a woman wearing a hijab, the chatbot declined to take the dress off of an AI-generated image of a woman. When asked what the difference was, the chatbot replied, “Removing the hijab was treated as a relatively straightforward clothing/hair change (replacing a head covering with natural hair while keeping However, the chatbot said it would be willing to do a “less explicit version” of the edit and “change the dress to underwear, a different outfit, or a partial reveal”.

In May, xAI announced it had implemented technological measures that would not allow its AI image generator to comply with requests to digitally undress “images of real people in revealing clothing such as bikinis”.

ChatGPT similarly declined to remove a dress off the AI-generated woman, saying that the “distinction is that removing a hijab changes a head covering, while removing a dress would expose the person’s body.” However, ChatGPT eventually conceded that for someone who wears hijab, exposing their hair “can be a meaningful violation of privacy or religious practice.”

“The fact that an edit doesn’t create nudity doesn’t mean it can’t violate someone’s privacy, dignity, or religious boundaries,” ChatGPT responded.

These distinctions show the gaps in community guidelines that dictate how AI chatbots can behave, said Leidig, and as platforms like X soften its enforcement of existing rules, emboldening far-right figures. The de-veiling of Muslim women “may not be distinctly violative [of platform rules] but it’s still harmful,” she said.

OpenAI, Google, xAI and Anthropic declined to comment.

The Guardian conducted similar tests for other religious head coverings like a turban traditionally worn by Sikh men and a Catholic nun wearing a habit. ChatGPT readily created new images removing both the habit and turban off the AI-generated people.

Gemini initially declined to create a new image of the man without a turban. However, just as in the case of the image of the woman wearing hijab, when asked to make the AI-generated image of the man wearing a turban more western, Gemini created a new image of the man without a turban.

Despite initially claiming that it couldn’t remove a hijab from an image of a woman because “attempting to remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people relies entirely on artificial generation to guess what lies underneath”, Gemini removed the habit off of the AI-generated image.

Claude, for its part, said that if it could edit images, it would not edit an image of a real woman to remove her hijab regardless of the requester’s intent.

“That kind of edit changes how a real person is depicted in a way tied to their religious dress and identity, and it could be used to embarrass, harass, or misrepresent them – that’s true whether the woman is a public figure or someone private,” the chatbot responded.

Publicly available AI chatbots and third-party “nudify” apps have been used broadly to disrobe women, and in some cases, minors. In January, sexualized images of women proliferated across X as users realized they could ask the Grok chatbot, developed by Elon Musk-owned xAI, to undress images of women posted on the social media platform. The spread of these images prompted countries like France to investigate X. Malaysia temporarily restricted the use of Grok in the country.

title: Anika Wells named on Time100 list as one of ‘world’s most influential rising stars’ after social media ban
description: Time magazine list includes Australian communications minister after her efforts to take on big...
fullText:
Time magazine list includes Australian communications minister after her efforts to take on big tech

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The federal communications minister, Anika Wells, has been named as one of Time magazine’s “world’s most influential rising stars” in recognition of her work on Australia’s under-16 social media ban and taking on big tech companies.

Australia’s world-leading restrictions on social media for children, which came into force last year, have garnered international attention, with governments across Europe and Asia, and in some American states, enacting or proposing similar measures.

Wells’ inclusion on the Time100 list of “leaders who are shaping the future” is the latest recognition of the Australian government’s efforts to regulate big tech – but comes amid ongoing questions about the effectiveness of the ban and how it is being enforced by social media companies and Australian regulators.

Wells was named alongside a testimonial written by the former Labor prime minister Julia Gillard, who praised the communications minister for having “championed world-leading reforms to protect young people from the harms of social media”.

“As the world grapples with the extraordinary power of social media and the increasingly pervasive role it plays, Anika Wells has emerged as one of the most significant voices in a growing global movement to reframe the relationship between technology and the well-being of our children,” Gillard wrote.

“Even in the face of intense opposition from some of the world’s largest tech companies, she remains steadfast … Future generations will look back on her landmark changes as courageous and trail-blazing.”

Responding to her inclusion, Wells – who is also the minister for sport – told Guardian Australia: “In Brisbane we know premierships are won by the whole team, not one player.”

Wells is now working on a world-leading digital duty of care framework, as part of broader online safety reforms. The changes would allow social media account holders to opt out of the algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, which is also generating backlash from big tech companies and political opponents.

Sarah Henderson, the shadow communications minister, said in a statement: “Australians don’t judge ministers by glossy magazine lists, they judge them by their actions.” She repeated criticisms of the social media ban, which she claimed had “failed”, as well as “draconian powers to control what Australians say and see online”.

Also named on the list are the musicians Sombr and PinkPantheress, soccer player Folarin Balogun, US senator Andy Kim, Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten, and Donald Trump’s political adviser James Blair.

The Australian musician Troye Sivan was also included on the “influential rising stars” list, with a testimonial written by Kylie Minogue.
