The five titles that got away as Evans seeks WRC glory
description: As Elfyn Evans looks to finally clinch the World Rally Championship title in Sardinia, BBC Sport looks back at the five times he finished runner-up.
fullText:
Few leading sports stars have been so tantalisingly close to crowning glory for so long without achieving ultimate success as rally driver Elfyn Evans.

The 37-year-old from Dolgellau in north-west Wales has been runner-up in the World Rally Championship (WRC) five times in the past six years.

But that could all be about to change.

With this year's WRC calendar truncated by the removal of the planned Saudi Arabia finale, Evans takes a 17-point lead into the now season-ending Rally Italia Sardegna from 1-4 October.

If Evans can maintain his advantage over team-mates Sami Pajari and Oliver Solberg it will be a crowning moment for the Welshman, who would become only the third Briton to win the WRC title - joining Colin McRae and Richard Burns.

As he prepares to grasp history in Sardinia, BBC Sport looks back at the five times Evans fell just short of his dream.

No change for leader Evans after WRC drops finale

White, Netherlands, Evans and sport's other great runners-up

BBC to broadcast World Rally Championship from 2027

Evans does have a world title - winning the WRC Junior Championship in 2012 which earned him a full-time seat in M-Sport's Ford Fiesta.

However, it was a move to Toyota Gazoo Racing in 2020 that put his senior career into overdrive.

Only huge last-event misfortune cost him instant success in a season cut from 13 races to seven by the Covid-19 pandemic.

After placing third at Monte Carlo in his first Yaris outing, Evans and co-driver Scott Martin excelled at a weather-shortened second round to win Rally Sweden.

It put the Welshman top of the WRC driver's championship for the first time, and although record-breaking Sebastien Ogier would temporarily reclaim the lead, a second victory in Turkey saw Evans take at 14-point advantage over the Frenchman into the final event.

With 10 of the 16 stages complete, the less experienced of the two drivers remained on course for a maiden championship success.

But Evans' dream ended in devastating fashion when he crashed down a bank after being caught out by treacherous snow-covered mountain roads.

Ogier claimed a seventh world title by just eight points to leave his team-mate "gutted".

"When I braked on that, it was just like glass and there was no chance of us slowing down at all. It completely caught me by surprise," said Evans after the race, later admitting "it was a massive disappointment", which made him "more determined" for the year ahead.

Evans took that determination and experience into the new year and soon grabbed the lead in the season-opening Rallye Monte Carlo.

However, local favourite Ogier went on to win in Monaco, and then three more of the first six rounds to take a commanding grip of the 2021 championship.

The Welsh driver was not about to give up though. A second rally win of the season in Finland. and second place in the penultimate round at Rally Catalunya, once again forced the title race into a final-event decider at Monza.

With a potentially bridgeable gap of 17 points, the two Toyota rally crews swapped the lead throughout - but Ogier and co-driver Julien Ingrassia eventually came out on top to claim both the rally and the title.

"It's been a pretty OK year," a typically level-headed Evans reflected at the end of the race.

"Of course, I can't help but feel a little disappointed right now, you always look to the places you could've done better."

The following year could certainly have been much better - as Evans struggled with the newly introduced hybrid cars.

Going off the road in the opening round and forced to retire from three further rallies, Evans finished 2022 in fourth place, more than 120 points behind first-time champion Kalle Rovanpera.

"2022 fell below our expectations," a defiant Evans told the BBC before the 2023 campaign.

"We're coming into the new season looking for improvements - and we're hoping we can challenge for the title."

And challenge he did - winning round four in Croatia to take a share of the championship lead, tied with Ogier and one point ahead of Rovanperra.

However, a crash at Rally Portugal set his title bid back as he was forced to retire in round five and - despite a victory in Finland - Evans had to concede the title with one round to go.

A crash and a disappointing finish at the Central European Rally may have handed back-to-back titles to Finnish team-mate Rovanpera, but the Welshman was to end the season on a high.

Victory at Rally Japan was his third of the campaign - the best return in any season to date for Evans who declared "it feels nice after last year".

With Rovanpera following Ogier's lead for 2024 in deciding not to contest a full calendar, surely this would be the year their Toyota team-mate would finally get to stand atop the WRC podium?

Sadly for Evans, the opening paragraph of the BBC report for the season's first race set the tone.

'Elfyn Evans faded to finish a disappointing third behind winner Thierry Neuville at Rallye Monte Carlo.'

As it turned out it was second place in the driver's championship come December, but it was another disappointing season for the Welsh driver, with Neuville instead becoming a first-time world champion after Evans' years of waiting.

And Evans, of course, was runner-up - though only just.

As Neuville lined up in Nagoya needing just six points - he collected 17 - to end his own streak of five championship runners-up spots, the Welshman began Rally Japan in third place.

For the second year in a row, Evans saved his best for last and a back-to-back Japanese victory brought a double silver lining.

Not only did it see him overhaul Ott Tanak to claim runners-up spot for a fourth time, it also saw Toyota snatch the manufacturer's championship.

However, the big personal prize remained as elusive as ever.

"We're sorry we couldn't deliver [the drivers'] championship," Evans said, "but we'll try again next year."

A revamp of the points system for 2025 was welcomed by Evans; it also brought his tightest title race yet.

After second place to Ogier in the Monte Carlo curtain-raiser, the re-energised Welshman won in Sweden and Kenya - rallies the Frenchman sat out.

With a 36-point advantage, Evans had opened up the largest championship lead ever recorded after three rounds of a WRC campaign.

But he would not win again that season and though he never finished lower than sixth, Ogier gradually whittled away at his lead until it came down to just three points with one round to go.

That race was a brand new entry to the calendar, and there was uncertainty over what lay ahead at Rally Saudi Arabia.

The terrain proved brutal for all the drivers. Tyre problems galore saw the leaderboard shifting like the sand. It ended with Ogier in third and Evans in sixth.

The points-swing was seven. The Frenchman had won a record-equalling ninth WRC title by four points, and Evans had fallen just short for the fifth time in six years.

"We've done what we can, that's it," was his reaction.

"We're competitors at the end of the day, we always want better, we always want more."

But there is only one more thing to do. Finally shake-off the tag of nearly-man.

He grabbed the 2026 championship lead with victory in February's Rally Sweden and has refused to let it go.

Once again his rivals are Toyota team-mates. This time it is Pajari, who won three rallies in a row, before Solberg triumphed in Rally Chile at the start of September to put himself back in the title reckoning.

Evans will require at most 19 points to guarantee him the title, but has not finished higher than third in the past five rallies since winning in Japan.

He will also have to cope with being first on the road in Sardinia - sweeping the gravel which has frequently caused him trouble in the past.

"I think especially with opening the road, normally in Sardinia it's a significant disadvantage to run first," concedes Evans who says he will "ignore the championship situation".

"You can't really afford to [think about the lead]. I have plenty of experience of what not to do," he muses.

"But you know how it turns out. I think it's far less certain than what it appears on paper."

True, but maybe by Sunday, the paper in the history books will show Evans finally proved he is not just another runner-up.

title: Ronaldo leaves Portugal camp after coach denies rift
description: Cristiano Ronaldo says he has left Portugal's international camp and will explain why "in time", hours after head coach Jorge Jesus denied any rift with the player.
fullText:
Cristiano Ronaldo says he has left Portugal's international camp and will explain the reasons why "in time".

It comes after head coach Jorge Jesus earlier said there was no rift with the captain, following claims the five-times Ballon d'Or winner had refused to train.

Ronaldo has said he considered retiring from international football after the World Cup in the summer but opted to continue as he chases down 1,000 career goals.

He was included in Jesus' 25-man squad for the current international break and started the opening Nations League game against Wales.

However, the Al-Nassr forward did not feature in Portugal's 2-1 win over Norway in Olso on Sunday and did not join his team-mates in going over to the visiting fans at the final whistle.

Instead, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United player headed to the changing rooms - prompting reports he was unhappy with the manager.

Speaking to media before Portugal's Nations League match against Denmark on Thursday, Jesus said: "There was no incident whatsoever.

"Any player - and I was a player myself - when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don't get on, no-one is happy about that."

Jesus said he had told Ronaldo before the match he would not be starting, but might be brought on later in the game.

"Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It's nothing to make a fuss about," he added.

Former Benfica manager Jesus also dismissed suggestions Ronaldo had refused to train on Tuesday, saying the 41-year-old instead had to do individual exercises for "mobility" and "strengthening" but would train as normal on Wednesday.

However, Ronaldo did not join his team-mates on the pitch in Denmark with Portuguese media sharing a video of him leaving Parken stadium alongside two members of the backroom staff.

And the player later took to Instagram to announce his departure.

"After the press conference of the national team and following a conversation with the president of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp," he wrote.

"In time, I will tell all the Portuguese the truth about the reasons that motivated me to leave."

He added he wished his team-mates good luck in their forthcoming games.

Goncalo Ramos scored the winner against Norway and Jesus had said the AC Milan striker would again be preferred to Ronaldo against Denmark.

"If I need [Ronaldo], he'll come on. If I don't need him, he won't."

The Portuguese Football Federation later confirmed Ronaldo's departure in a statement which added: "Preparation for the two matches against Denmark and Norway continue as planned with the 24 remaining squad members.

"The entire delegation remains totally focussed on the national team's next fixtures and on achieving the established objectives."

What will new call-ups bring to Northern Ireland?
description: Before the upcoming 2027 Women's World Cup play-off with Portugal, what will the five new faces bring to Northern Ireland?
fullText:
When Northern Ireland run out to take on Portugal in their 2027 Women's World Cup play-off, they know they will be the underdogs.

That would be the case even if Michael McArdle had a full-strength squad to pick from, but he has had to deal with a lengthy injury list before the first play-off round.

However, disappointment for some leads to opportunities for others, and his 23-strong squad as produced five new names.

Sparta Pargue forward Kess Elmore was a surprise inclusion but her versatility could be key, while Galway United defender Lucy-Jayne Grant is another new face.

McArdle has also rewarded three Women's Premiership players - Naomi McLaughlin, Jane McMaster and Charlotte Havern - with their first call-ups.

But what can they all bring to the international stage?

Elmore and Grant named in Northern Ireland squad

With the absence of key attackers Simone Magill, who is back in training after having her first child, and Danielle Maxwell and Caragh Hamilton, who are injured, the introduction of Elmore to the squad is intriguing.

The 27-year-old Sparta Prague attacker qualifies for Northern Ireland through her father, who is from Lisburn.

Elmore came through Liverpool's academy and made the move to the USA in 2017 to play college football for the UConn Huskies and Oregon Ducks.

Her professional career started with Saint Etienne in France in 2023 and moved to Brooklyn FC for the inaugural USL Super League the following year.

Elmore has Champions League experience with Austrian champions St Polten against the likes of Chelsea and Lyon, and she moved to the Czech Republic in July.

Predominantly an attacking midfielder, Elmore can play right across the forward line and McArdle says "that versatility brings a strength to us".

"The biggest thing for Kess is the attacking prowess she's got as a creative player and an attacking player," said the Scot.

"She's coming in with good experience of playing against high quality opposition, and Portugal's squad is full of players that are at elite European clubs.

"Not speaking on behalf of Kess, but when you get that first call up at the age of 27 it is quite a special moment.

"It's been quite a special few weeks working with Kess in the background, so I'm looking forward to her joining camp and bringing those qualities to the group."

As well as Elmore, another player who has earned their first call-up is Cavan-born left back Lucy-Jayne Grant, who qualifies for Northern Ireland through her father.

The 22-year-old plays for Galway United in the League of Ireland, and she helped the club win the cross-border All-Island Cup in 2024.

McArdle said he had identified Grant for a possible call-up early into this time at the job, and she had earned her chance after he and his staff done their "due diligence".

"Over the summer she's performed well and she has spent time in the environment as a training player, so we have got to know her.

"She has broken through now on the left side of defence, so she'll add to the depth within there with the squad."

As well as her on-pitch ability, Galway's website says that Grant can juggle and is a qualified piano and violin teacher, so should be able to entertain the camp throughout the window.

Women's Premiership players featuring in senior Northern Ireland squads is nothing new.

In fact, before the historic Euro 2022 finals, it was the norm.

While more players have moved to England or Scotland over the past few years, the Irish League still plays a key role for the international team.

In McArdle's squad for the play-off, eight of his players are still based in Northern Ireland, and he has handed three of them first call-ups.

Attacking midfielder McLaughlin, 20, broke through at Sion Swifts before she moved to Cliftonville in 2024.

Her performances at Solitude earned her a move to Aberdeen in January but she returned to Northern Ireland with Glentoran in July, where she has impressed.

"Naomi has had a real purple patch since returning to Glentoran," McArdle said.

"It is exciting for her. She gives us another attacking option and a bit of versatility because she's slightly different to some of the players that are in the squad."

Full back McMaster, 22, has been a stalwart at Linfield and has been a key player in the club's push into title contention this season.

McMaster, who can also play in the centre of defence, has represented Northern Ireland before both at underage level and with the futsal team, but this is her opportunity to win a first senior cap.

"Jane has had a few consistent seasons and come through the international pathway," said McArdle.

"She is having a fantastic season with Linfield and deserves her call-up, which is exciting."

At 16, Havern is the youngest players in McArdle's squad and has earned a call-up after helping Cliftonville to a Premiership and League Cup double, and the Reds are also in the Irish Cup final.

Another underage international, it will be a chance for McArdle to work with the all-action midfielder first hand in the senior squad.

"Charlotte's impressive form with Cliftonville and has been a key part of their performances this season.

"They have helped Charlotte break through into the national team to get this experience."

title: Tom Curry extends Sale Sharks contract
description: England international flanker Tom Curry signs a two-year contract extension with Sale Sharks.
fullText:
England international flanker Tom Curry has signed a two-year contract extension with Sale Sharks.

The 28-year-old has spent his entire career with the Sharks and made his debut aged 18 in October 2016 and his new deal will keep him with the Prem side until the end of the 2027-28 campaign.

Director of rugby Alex Sanderson said Curry, whose identical twin brother Ben also plays for the club, is "fundamental" to the team.

"The terms are a couple of years and that's on Tom's desire to ensure that he's physically in the best spot to be able to honour his contract, to play a load of games for the next two years," Sanderson said.

"Then we both said we'll see where his body's at, at that point, with the want and desire for him to finish his career at Sale.

"He was the one, after some really honest conversations, that said we need to keep this group together, the core group together.

"He's fundamental to us, in terms of being the keystone, really, to that whole group."

Curry added: "Sale Sharks means everything to me and this is the club I have supported my whole life.

"I'm very proud of the hard work we've put in over the last 10 years to get the club to where it is now, but I know how much more we have to give and that's the reason I want to stay. There's no place I would rather be."

Curry, who has been capped 71 times by his country, missed the majority of the 2023-24 season after being diagnosed with femoroacetabular impingement syndrome - a condition that means the ball in the hip joint is not entirely round.

He underwent hip surgery in February 2024 and was warned his career could be over but returned to playing top level rugby just four months later.

In December of that year he had a stem-cell procedure with a view to him being able to play until the 2027 World Cup in Australia.

"He's surpassing expectations, his own medical expectations and what's gone before him in terms of the [hip] injury that he had," Sanderson added.

"We're not seeing any signs of wear and tear at this point and it might come in to factor later down the line but at this point he's as fresh and as mobile as he's ever been."

Meanwhile, Sharks summer signing Courtney Lawes, who made his Prem debut for the side in the 34-24 home defeat by Bristol at the weekend, said earlier this month that players who choose to go abroad should remain eligible for England selection.

Lawes, has won 105 England caps and returned to England this summer, having spent two years at French side Brive where he was ineligible to represent his country.

At present, the Rugby Football Union does not permit players not playing in this country to be picked for Steve Borthwick's national side, other than in exceptional circumstances.

Toulouse back row Jack Willis, who has retained his award as the best player in France's Top 14, has not played for England since 2023 but said this week "it's something I still want to do".

However, Exeter Chiefs director of rugby Rob Baxter has said he does not think the rules should be changed and Sanderson said altering the approach could lead to the Prem being "devastated".

"I just think it would devalue our the Prem, which we know is a really good product with really competitive teams, too much if players were allowed to take the pay cheque, move to France and then get the Eurostar over for training with the international team," he said.

"I think it would devastate the Prem because then players can literally have the cake and eat it, can't they? They can take the pay cheque and there'll be no consequence for playing outside of the country.

"I understand the views of those lads who feel otherwise and we have some in our quarters.

"I'm looking at from a different point of view, from a director of rugby that wants the players and we wouldn't be able to compete to keep them on the books if we had to go against some of the juggernauts of the Top 14."

title: Ex-world champion boxer Liam Smith charged with GBH
description: The 38-year-old was arrested after an alleged attack on an apartment building's night concierge.
fullText:
Former world champion boxer Liam Smith has been charged with causing grievous bodily harm after an alleged attack on a night concierge at a luxury Manchester apartment building.

Smith, who held the WBO light-middleweight title from 2015 to 2016, was arrested after the man suffered serious facial injuries at The Blade on Silvercroft Street in Deansgate on 13 September, police confirmed.

The 38-year-old appeared at Manchester Magistrates Court the following day charged with causing GBH with intent, and was released on bail.

Smith, from Liverpool, is next due to appear at Manchester Crown Court on 19 October, where he will be asked to enter a plea.

The alleged victim reportedly suffered fractures and required surgery.

Smith, nicknamed Beefy, had been due to make a comeback fight against local fighter Ilaru Kujala in Finland on 4 September.

However, he withdrew from the fight a few days earlier after suffering a calf injury, according to reports.

Smith has fought at the highest levels, including against elite champions such as Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez.

More recently he fought British rival Chris Eubank Jr in two memorable bouts, defeating the Brighton man in the first fight in January 2023 before suffering a defeat in the rematch eight months later.

fullText:
Crude oil is moving through the Strait of Hormuz at a pace that is starting to approach prewar levels, a notable rebound for the world's most critical oil choke point.

That restored flow is mainly the result of Iran's somewhat depleted military capability and a U.S. Navy operation that has secured a portion of the waterway for relatively secure passage.

But the forces driving high fuel prices are not receding along with the development. That will require a lot more than the costly military campaign that is clearing the way for passage of one product at one particular moment in the war.

Most of the refined gasoline and diesel that was moving through the strait before the war is still not getting shipped, a major factor keeping prices elevated.

The rebound of crude shipments "is good news, but we are far from out of the woods," said Bob McNally, founder of the research firm Rapidan Energy Group. "The market realizes that. We have dug ourselves into a deep deficit over the last several months, and this only reduces it. It does not get us back to where we were."

Crude oil prices dipped Tuesday - largely as a response to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline resuming limited operations. The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, remained above $100 a barrel Wednesday morning, roughly 40 percent higher than it was when the Iran war began in February.

The outlook for the war and for oil was further clouded on Wednesday, when the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported that three vessels carrying fuel through a corridor of the strait the U.S. military has been trying to protect had been attacked the day before.

Meanwhile, the price of a gallon of regular gas in the United States is averaging $4.43, and diesel is at $6.41, according to AAA.

Analysts warn that even sustained deliveries of crude through the Strait of Hormuz at prewar levels would not do much to meaningfully bring down global prices in the coming weeks.

They note that oil inventories are depleted and need to be replenished. Refining infrastructure in the Middle East has been badly damaged and will take time to repair - all the while remaining vulnerable to further attacks.

As a result of that constrained capacity, gasoline and diesel shipments through the strait - crucial to bringing prices down for consumers - remain just a fraction of what they were before the war.

"Nobody consumes crude oil directly," said Mark Finley, an oil markets scholar at Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy. "It has to be made into something useful, like diesel or jet fuel or gasoline. The world's refining system that turns crude oil into useful products is severely strained."

As if to punctuate the point that the emergency is not over and inventories of everything are running low, the U.S. Energy Department on Tuesday announced it would release another 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is already at its lowest level since 1983.

"We have dug ourselves into a big hole," Finley said.

There is general agreement in the oil industry that most of the crude still getting blocked in the Strait of Hormuz is Iranian, and that is by design. The U.S. is trying to put economic pressure on the regime and choke off its funding stream for its military activities.

As far as how much non-Iranian crude is getting through, ship tracking firms offer somewhat different estimates.

According to Kpler, the week ending Sept. 27 averaged nearly 12.5 million barrels per day, just 1 million barrels below the "pre-war baseline."

Windward, another ship tracking platform, estimated closer to 10 million barrels per day.

"This is not trivial," said Ami Daniel, Windward's co-founder and CEO. "The U.S. military has done a fantastic job facilitating consistent shipments."

The amount of oil getting through, though, does continue to swing wildly. There were days in September where only a few million barrels transited the strait, according to ship tracking data.

The restored flows depend on extremely costly U.S. Navy assistance and dark-fleet work-arounds that could unravel with a renewed Iranian military campaign.

Markets remain skeptical that the shipments of crude can continue at prewar levels absent a major diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran.

"Maintaining the American military presence required to keep significant volumes of oil moving through the Strait comes at an enormous financial and operational cost," Danny Citrinowicz, a Middle East security scholar at the Atlantic Council, posted Tuesday on X.

"The real test is whether Washington can turn its military advantage into a durable situation in which oil flows normally, insurance and transportation costs decline, the extraordinary U.S. military deployment can be reduced, and Iran effectively loses Hormuz as a tool of strategic coercion," Citrinowicz wrote. "We are not there yet."

Even full restoration of shipping through the strait, McNally warned, would not bring markets back to where they were at the beginning of the year.

Iran has shifted its attacks away from the strait toward oil infrastructure on land, which in some cases can be even more damaging. One such recent attack disabled Saudi Arabia's key East-West pipeline, which had been delivering 7 million barrels of crude each day. The pipeline has been only partially restored, and analysts say it remains extremely vulnerable to further targeting.

"Iran may be losing control of Hormuz, but it retains the ability to disable critical infrastructure," McNally said. "This progress can be quickly offset by the Iranians and their allies hitting those fixed assets."

Karen DeYoung contributed to this report.
